rnafoundry.com/yash, Made at the RNA Foundry.
In January 2025, 32-year-old Yashdeep Bindal was diagnosed with stage IV pancreatic cancer. He had just returned to work after the birth of his daughter, Maya.
At the RNA Foundry, we are developing a personalized cancer vaccine for Yash. We’re sharing his tumour sequencing data and our vaccine design so that other researchers can help refine it.
Design #2 is our lead vaccine design for Yash. It was generated using matched-normal white-blood-cell DNA alongside tumour DNA and RNA. We share the code, methods, results and sequencing-data access instructions so others can reproduce the work and explore alternative designs.
Design #2 combines 12 mutation, 5 splice, 5 CTA/self and 2 fusion regions. Independent paired Mutect2 discovery, direct normal evidence and tumour-RNA reconstruction support its mutation selection. All 12 eligible mutation regions are included, with no top-N expression-weighted cutoff. Seven original mutation targets were detected in normal DNA and removed; AQP3 and TGFBR2 regions were added. Patient-supported SEC/MITD routing sequences and jointly optimized order/linkers form the protein, which is synonymously encoded with the recorded PopRNA settings. PolyA and any downstream extension are unspecified; nucleotide files contain known upstream segments, not complete molecular sequences. This is one research approach; alternative analyses, antigen selections and designs are welcome.
- Selected antigens and sequences.
- Final protein, antigen order and component coordinates.
- Known RNA segment, coding DNA and annotated DNA segment.
- Methods, every-antigen review and comparison with Design #1.
- Junction check, hydropathy screen, nucleotide verification and completion audit.
FASTA and TSV files are plain text. JSON records inputs, methods and checks. The individual evidence review retains sparse RNA support, RNA-source uncertainties and the encoder's unmet soft folding target alongside the checks that passed.
Use Python 3.11 or 3.12, from the repository root:
python3.11 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e '.[mrna]'
yash-vaccine verify
yash-vaccine reproduce --output work/design-2-replay
The first command checks Design #2’s recorded evidence and annotations. The second replays selection, joint order/linker optimization from recorded costs, independent junction checks and synonymous encoding. It compares the selected, protein and nucleotide outputs byte for byte. Neither downloads patient reads, runs new model inference or starts cloud jobs. Repeating raw-read processing or model inference is a separate scope; the Design #2 guide records the Modal controllers, dependencies and large-data locations.
yash-vaccine reproduce defaults to the lead Design #2. Use
yash-vaccine reproduce designs/initial for Design #1. Its
guide and the usage guide explain the
earlier workflow. yash-vaccine compare designs/initial designs/design-2 compares
the two complete proteins by stable region identity.
yash-vaccine init my-candidate
This creates a README and a starter run.py in designs/my-candidate/. Describe your question and implement your approach using any code or tools you need. Reuse our data and helpers where useful, or develop a different workflow. Then run your script as described in its README, for example:
python designs/my-candidate/run.py
Keep your results with your notes: an antigen table, analysis, cassette or whatever you produced. There is no required recipe or pipeline. A design might contain:
designs/my-candidate/
  README.md          Question, methods, inputs, commands and findings
  run.py             Your analysis (or another script/workflow)
  selected.tsv       Chosen antigens, if produced
  cassette.fasta     Construct, if assembled
To change the lead Design #2, use its methods,
candidate pool and
selected regions as starting points
for your own script. reproduce checks the recorded lead; it is not a configurable
runner for a changed antigen set.
The optional Design #1 recipe runner varies the earlier tumour-only selection and internal cassette. It does not use Design #2's matched-normal evidence or produce its complete SEC/MITD and RNA stages.
Have a vaccine design for Yash? Submit a pull request. Fork the repository,
create a branch and add your work under designs/. Include your selected antigens
and rationale, sequences where produced, code and reproduction instructions, and
results. Label unspecified components explicitly. The
contribution guide explains what to include and how to submit it.
- Clinical reports: Stanford pathology/IHC and STAMP, Caris tumour profiling, and Guardant360 liquid biopsy PDFs.
- Data: what is included, what is stored externally, and how to obtain it.
- Matched-normal DNA and Design #2 data: final normal BAM, scoped genotypes, paired calls, QC and exact references; original normal FASTQs excluded.
- Design #2 methods: scientific decisions and evidence behind the lead design.
- Design #1 methods: the earlier design generated without matched-normal DNA.
- Usage: reproduce our candidate or develop your own approach.
- Contribute a design: what to include in a design pull request.
- Upstream stages: DNA/RNA discovery and native scoring contracts.
- AGENTS.md: a short map for coding agents.
The shared data support many approaches beyond these designs:
- MHC class II: class-II presentation and CD4 T-cell targets.
- Immunogenicity: predictions of T-cell responses alongside binding scores.
- Processing and presentation: antigen order and linkers optimized for intended target presentation, alongside the current unwanted-junction binding objective.
- Antigen trafficking: compare the current SEC–antigens–MITD architecture with other routing elements or a cassette without them.
Provenance maps the input, model and verification records. Large sequencing files and case-analysis outputs are available through a public read-only endpoint. Download instructions and the file catalog describe the files, sizes and checksums. Third-party tools, models and references come from their providers. Full upstream RNA modules are not bundled; local replay uses included evidence and recorded predictions. Required credits and retained-source notices cover the materials used here.

Gemini Decisions API
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
18:32:42 UTC
03:32:42 KST

Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions
Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio.
The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed.
Strong performance and calibration
On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error.
Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.
Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass
Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.
You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:
- noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.
- choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate.
- score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.
The input field uses the same Content block format as the Interactions API. Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request:
from google import genai
client = genai.Client(http_options={"api_version": "v1beta"})
result = client.decisions.create(
    model="gemini-decision-1",
    input=[{
            "type": "image",
            "uri": "https://storage.googleapis.com/generativeai-downloads/images/spill.jpg",
            "mime_type": "image/jpeg",
        },
        {
            "type": "text",
            "text": "Breakroom counter check before the 9 AM client meeting.",
        },
    ],
    questions={
        "has_spill": {
            "type": "noul",
            "instructions": "Is there an uncleaned liquid spill on the counter?",
        },
        "next_action": {
            "type": "choice",
            "instructions": "Which cleanup action fits the scene?",
            "criteria": {
                "wipe_with_cloth": "Small counter spill with a cloth or towel already nearby.",
                "dispatch_janitorial": "Large floor hazard, broken glass, or active leak.",
                "ready_for_meeting": "Counter is clean and ready.",
            },
        },
        "severity": {
            "type": "score",
            "instructions": "Rate the severity of the counter mess.",
            "criteria": [
                "Clean and ready.",
                "Minor localized spill.",
                "Major spill or safety hazard.",
            ],
        },
    },
)
How teams are building with the Decisions API
Teams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls:
- Dynamic model routing in Gemini Notebook: Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router to instantly direct incoming queries to the optimal model tier and thinking level for each request. The Decisions API classifies intent in milliseconds to serve everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency while reserving deep reasoning models for complex tasks.
- Rapid design iteration in Stitch: The new rapid canvas experiment in Stitch uses the Decisions API to generate playable wireframes of a product flow in seconds and to apply edits made by voice or tap almost instantly. When the flow feels right, one click hands the screens off to the full Stitch experience for deeper design polish.
- Emoji selection in CC: CC from Google Labs uses the Decisions API to pick the right emoji reaction from a palette of more than 200 options in a fraction of a second, so reactions appear instantly without adding latency.
- Safety layer for MCP tools in Search: Google Search uses the Decision API to detect adversarial behavior and content against adversarial evals with high efficacy within the latency envelope.
Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed).
Start building today
Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in Google AI Studio for prototyping. Your shared input is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs.
You can start building today by grabbing an API key in Google AI Studio, trying our Doorstep Parcels, Speed Sketch, and Find the Zoo Keeper demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the Decisions API documentation.
Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across OpenRouter, LangChain, Vercel, LiteLLM, Pydantic AI, Pipecat, LiveKit, and OpenCode alongside the google-genai SDKs, with support coming soon to Gemini in Google Cloud.

AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
18:28:31 UTC
03:28:31 KST

AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
In 2004, barely a month into my new job at Amazon, I got the opportunity to pick an intern to join my team. I had an advantage over my colleagues: I had already heard about a brilliant young man working toward his PhD at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam (where I happened to have received mine as well :-)). I immediately picked Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, whom you all now know as Swami. It was probably one of the best decisions I have made in my 22 years as Amazon’s CTO.
After a disastrous Christmas in 2004, when commercial relational databases could not scale to Amazon’s needs, I asked Swami to do a deep dive into how relational databases were actually used at Amazon. It turned out that 70% of database operations were not relational at all. They were key-value. That insight led to Dynamo, which Swami helped architect. When his internship was over, I hired him full-time right away, even before he had finished his PhD.
Bringing in another opinionated academic led to many fantastic discussions with Amazon’s practical engineers, who had become scale experts by actually building at scale. Eventual vs. strong consistency, CAP vs. Paxos, and more. Over time, Swami became one of the principal architects of AWS’s data strategy. And as we have seen in recent years, he has also been one of the intellectual drivers behind AI innovation at Amazon.
I am honoured that he wanted to write a guest post about the fundamental distributed systems work that sits behind many of AWS’s services, and about how the engineer’s work changes when agents write the code. AWS Emulator, launched today, gives agents the kind of test environment that work relied on. Swami’s story is another great example of invisible engineering.
Now, go build.
-W
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
Today we release AWS Emulator, which gives coding agents a local copy of AWS to test against, and it connects to a project from early in my career. In many ways, this emulator launch reminds me of the effort we put into reliable software engineering to improve the quality of the distributed systems we build. To that end, we wanted to share a story:
About twenty years ago, Werner asked me to work with one of Amazon’s earliest engineers, Al Vermeulen, on a distributed lock service we called “Alf”. Alf was built on Paxos, a protocol based on Leslie Lamport’s work that lets a group of servers agree on one value, and a replication engine in it kept copies of the data consistent across servers. Alf, to date, is the service that powers many of our complex distributed systems like S3, DynamoDB and many more (although it has evolved quite a bit with various changes on top – will save it for another blog!).
Distributed systems are hard to test
Paxos is the gold standard among distributed systems consensus protocols and was well understood in academia. However, building it at the scale Amazon and AWS were growing into was not easy. We had to deal with not just replication across servers and data centers but also tens of thousands of clients asking for locks at the same time, renewing their leases during network partitions all the while with the core requirement: Always be correct! At that time, the best ideas for testing distributed systems were large-scale system testing and chaos-based testing. Both worked, but they were expensive, and they could not reproduce many kinds of conditions on demand. That mattered for Alf, which was meant to be the truth store, giving every client a strongly consistent view of the truth, and which had to keep working through server failures and packet loss as well. Several industry papers had written that Paxos-based locking services were hard to get right, and the difficulty of testing them was part of the reason.
We addressed that by simulating Alf’s environment with as much fidelity as we could manage. We ran the servers inside a JVM and simulated the network and the rest of the infrastructure they depended on, so the whole system lived in one program that we controlled. We could drop packets and inject other faults whenever we chose, and we built tools that poked at the simulation for bugs and scalability problems. Concurrency bugs appear only when events happen in a particular order, and in the simulation we could set up many of those orderings on purpose and inspect how Alf handled each one. We also used formal reasoning, through theoretical techniques such as TLA+, and it found many issues as well. By testing this way we ironed out most of Alf’s concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing in a real environment then turned up different problems, because the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.
Outgrowing hand-built test environments
Simulation and formal reasoning both improved the software quality of the distributed systems we applied them to. The simulation worked because a small team could build a copy of one system’s environment by hand, and at the time AWS had only a small handful of services. But today AWS has over 200 services, and an application that calls AWS needs a test environment for each one it uses. Building all of those by hand would take years of engineering, and agents now write code far faster than any team can check it in production. So, we wanted to know whether agents could build and test those environments themselves.
The idea came from Matt Goldberg, a Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. His hypothesis was that, given a written description of how a service should behave and the real service to check against, an agent could build a working version of that service on its own. For AWS, the written description is the set of public API models, written in Smithy, AWS’s format for describing a service’s operations and their inputs, outputs, and errors. The real service to check against is the AWS cloud itself, the same system customers use.
The agents work from fidelity tests, which are end-to-end customer scenarios devised from the public API models. A test might check, for example, that in Amazon Simple Queue Service a received message stays hidden from other readers until its visibility timeout runs out. The agents correct each test until it passes against real AWS, so the test records how AWS behaves. The agents then build the emulator until it passes that same test, and a test that still fails points at a gap in the emulator. Matt began with SQS alone, and when he gave Kiro one prompt describing this approach, it returned a passable first version of an SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. Matt Goldberg’s launch post tells how that prototype grew into AWS Emulator. All of AWS Emulator’s code was written and tested by agents, and it is built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. It runs free and offline on your own machine. Teams of agents test it against real AWS and fix the gaps they find. Every change goes through a merge gate, a deep bench of automated checks that every change must pass before it enters the codebase, including several security agents doing adversarial reviews.
Infrastructure in the coding loop
A coding agent works in a loop: it writes code, runs it, and reads the result before deciding what to change next. In distributed systems that loop runs inside infrastructure, so the services it calls have to behave like the real ones. When they do, an agent can check its own work as it writes and produce correct code on its first attempt far more often, which improves software quality. AWS Emulator puts that infrastructure inside the loop on your own machine.
The engineer’s job when agents write the code
When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct. It was a lesson I learned the hard way when I used Kiro to rebuild the replication engine that Al and I had built for Alf, which took us about four months the first time. I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.
The agents building AWS Emulator had both from the start, in the public API models and in real AWS. An engineer built the scaffolding that runs them. An internal version came together over a weekend and started gaining adoption within a month. Turning that into a robust solution took much more work.
Software quality in the AI era depends on the guardrails that engineers design around agents. In AWS Emulator, those guardrails are the fidelity tests verified against real AWS, a merge gate with multiple security agents that each review a change for different ways to attack it alongside a general code reviewer, and deterministic checks that stop agents from touching code they are not supposed to. We expect agents to build and check most software, with engineers deciding what gets built and when the work is correct. We are early in learning how engineers drive teams of agents to build reliable, high-quality software, and the way AWS Emulator came to life is a good example of how that works in practice. We expect to keep adding guardrails and refining how the agents build it.
What to know at launch
The emulator code is released under CC0, a Creative Commons dedication to the public domain.
We will share more about this work at re:Invent. The full commit history and every issue the agents have filed are public in the GitHub repository, and its “things-that-do-not-work” folder holds the issues describing behaviors the agents found that do not yet match real AWS.

AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code

AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
In 2004, barely a month into my new job at Amazon, I got the opportunity to pick an intern to join my team. I had an advantage over my colleagues: I had already heard about a brilliant young man working toward his PhD at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam (where I happened to have received mine as well :-)). I immediately picked Swaminathan Sivasubramanian, whom you all now know as Swami. It was probably one of the best decisions I have made in my 22 years as Amazon’s CTO.
After a disastrous Christmas in 2004, when commercial relational databases could not scale to Amazon’s needs, I asked Swami to do a deep dive into how relational databases were actually used at Amazon. It turned out that 70% of database operations were not relational at all. They were key-value. That insight led to Dynamo, which Swami helped architect. When his internship was over, I hired him full-time right away, even before he had finished his PhD.
Bringing in another opinionated academic led to many fantastic discussions with Amazon’s practical engineers, who had become scale experts by actually building at scale. Eventual vs. strong consistency, CAP vs. Paxos, and more. Over time, Swami became one of the principal architects of AWS’s data strategy. And as we have seen in recent years, he has also been one of the intellectual drivers behind AI innovation at Amazon.
I am honoured that he wanted to write a guest post about the fundamental distributed systems work that sits behind many of AWS’s services, and about how the engineer’s work changes when agents write the code. AWS Emulator, launched today, gives agents the kind of test environment that work relied on. Swami’s story is another great example of invisible engineering.
Now, go build.
-W
AWS Emulator and the engineer's job when agents write the code
Today we release AWS Emulator, which gives coding agents a local copy of AWS to test against, and it connects to a project from early in my career. In many ways, this emulator launch reminds me of the effort we put into reliable software engineering to improve the quality of the distributed systems we build. To that end, we wanted to share a story:
About twenty years ago, Werner asked me to work with one of Amazon’s earliest engineers, Al Vermeulen, on a distributed lock service we called “Alf”. Alf was built on Paxos, a protocol based on Leslie Lamport’s work that lets a group of servers agree on one value, and a replication engine in it kept copies of the data consistent across servers. Alf, to date, is the service that powers many of our complex distributed systems like S3, DynamoDB and many more (although it has evolved quite a bit with various changes on top – will save it for another blog!).
Distributed systems are hard to test
Paxos is the gold standard among distributed systems consensus protocols and was well understood in academia. However, building it at the scale Amazon and AWS were growing into was not easy. We had to deal with not just replication across servers and data centers but also tens of thousands of clients asking for locks at the same time, renewing their leases during network partitions all the while with the core requirement: Always be correct! At that time, the best ideas for testing distributed systems were large-scale system testing and chaos-based testing. Both worked, but they were expensive, and they could not reproduce many kinds of conditions on demand. That mattered for Alf, which was meant to be the truth store, giving every client a strongly consistent view of the truth, and which had to keep working through server failures and packet loss as well. Several industry papers had written that Paxos-based locking services were hard to get right, and the difficulty of testing them was part of the reason.
We addressed that by simulating Alf’s environment with as much fidelity as we could manage. We ran the servers inside a JVM and simulated the network and the rest of the infrastructure they depended on, so the whole system lived in one program that we controlled. We could drop packets and inject other faults whenever we chose, and we built tools that poked at the simulation for bugs and scalability problems. Concurrency bugs appear only when events happen in a particular order, and in the simulation we could set up many of those orderings on purpose and inspect how Alf handled each one. We also used formal reasoning, through theoretical techniques such as TLA+, and it found many issues as well. By testing this way we ironed out most of Alf’s concurrency bugs before it ran on real servers. Testing in a real environment then turned up different problems, because the real world exposes things a simulation cannot.
Outgrowing hand-built test environments
Simulation and formal reasoning both improved the software quality of the distributed systems we applied them to. The simulation worked because a small team could build a copy of one system’s environment by hand, and at the time AWS had only a small handful of services. But today AWS has over 200 services, and an application that calls AWS needs a test environment for each one it uses. Building all of those by hand would take years of engineering, and agents now write code far faster than any team can check it in production. So, we wanted to know whether agents could build and test those environments themselves.
The idea came from Matt Goldberg, a Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team. His hypothesis was that, given a written description of how a service should behave and the real service to check against, an agent could build a working version of that service on its own. For AWS, the written description is the set of public API models, written in Smithy, AWS’s format for describing a service’s operations and their inputs, outputs, and errors. The real service to check against is the AWS cloud itself, the same system customers use.
The agents work from fidelity tests, which are end-to-end customer scenarios devised from the public API models. A test might check, for example, that in Amazon Simple Queue Service a received message stays hidden from other readers until its visibility timeout runs out. The agents correct each test until it passes against real AWS, so the test records how AWS behaves. The agents then build the emulator until it passes that same test, and a test that still fails points at a gap in the emulator. Matt began with SQS alone, and when he gave Kiro one prompt describing this approach, it returned a passable first version of an SQS emulator in about 15 minutes. Matt Goldberg’s launch post tells how that prototype grew into AWS Emulator. All of AWS Emulator’s code was written and tested by agents, and it is built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. It runs free and offline on your own machine. Teams of agents test it against real AWS and fix the gaps they find. Every change goes through a merge gate, a deep bench of automated checks that every change must pass before it enters the codebase, including several security agents doing adversarial reviews.
Infrastructure in the coding loop
A coding agent works in a loop: it writes code, runs it, and reads the result before deciding what to change next. In distributed systems that loop runs inside infrastructure, so the services it calls have to behave like the real ones. When they do, an agent can check its own work as it writes and produce correct code on its first attempt far more often, which improves software quality. AWS Emulator puts that infrastructure inside the loop on your own machine.
The engineer’s job when agents write the code
When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct. It was a lesson I learned the hard way when I used Kiro to rebuild the replication engine that Al and I had built for Alf, which took us about four months the first time. I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.
The agents building AWS Emulator had both from the start, in the public API models and in real AWS. An engineer built the scaffolding that runs them. An internal version came together over a weekend and started gaining adoption within a month. Turning that into a robust solution took much more work.
Software quality in the AI era depends on the guardrails that engineers design around agents. In AWS Emulator, those guardrails are the fidelity tests verified against real AWS, a merge gate with multiple security agents that each review a change for different ways to attack it alongside a general code reviewer, and deterministic checks that stop agents from touching code they are not supposed to. We expect agents to build and check most software, with engineers deciding what gets built and when the work is correct. We are early in learning how engineers drive teams of agents to build reliable, high-quality software, and the way AWS Emulator came to life is a good example of how that works in practice. We expect to keep adding guardrails and refining how the agents build it.

We will share more about this work at re:Invent. The full commit history and every issue the agents have filed are public in the GitHub repository, and its “things-that-do-not-work” folder holds the issues describing behaviors the agents found that do not yet match real AWS.

AWS Finally Built Its Own AWS Emulator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
18:21:38 UTC
03:21:38 KST

AWS Emulator is a local emulator of the AWS APIs. You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS.
The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead.
AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See Security in AWS Emulator.
Documentation: AWS Emulator User Guide
Install the aws-emulator skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See Getting started with an AI coding agent.
aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1
- Linux: install the RPM or Debian package and run aws-emulator. See Getting started on Linux.
- Windows / macOS: run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See Getting started with Docker.
Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator.
Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See Getting started with embedded mode, and Building from source below for its build cost.
To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the releases page. To check whether your own project is expected to work, see Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator.
Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's issues/ directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under issues/things-that-do-not-work/, and ones that have since been fixed move to issues/things-that-now-work/.
You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see Quick start). Building from source is supported on Linux (x86_64 and aarch64); on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above.
- A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via rustup).
- A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code.
- At least 100 GB of free disk for target/. The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added.
- A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster.
cargo build -p aws-emulator-router
cargo run   -p aws-emulator-router
The emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297 (self-signed certificate).
Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first cargo test builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and target/ on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one CARGO_TARGET_DIR across projects, cache target/ (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change.
.
├── Cargo.toml              # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates
├── services/
│   └── service-<name>/     # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE
│       ├── smithy-model/   # <name>.json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol
│       ├── build.rs        # generates the service declaration from the model
│       ├── src/
│       │   ├── service.rs  # request routing and refusal overrides
│       │   ├── state.rs    # this service's in-memory state
│       │   └── ops/        # one file per operation
│       └── tests/
├── core/
│   ├── router/             # the emulator binary: mounts every service on one endpoint
│   └── embedded/           # the in-process (embedded mode) facade
├── vendor/                 # framework crates — do not edit (replaced on update)
└── issues/                 # tracked fidelity issues
AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default. AWS Emulator collects telemetry data with strict data minimization in mind, preventing identification or attribution to specific users, accounts, or organizations. Its records never include what’s in your requests or responses, your code, your credentials, or personal data. We don’t share telemetry with third parties.
For details on what is collected and how the data is handled, see Telemetry in AWS Emulator. To turn telemetry off, use one of the following options.
Start the emulator with the --telemetry option (short form -t) set to off. This setting applies only to that emulator process.
aws-emulator --telemetry off
In a container, add --telemetry off after the image name in the docker run command.
Set EMULATOR_TELEMETRY to off before you start the emulator. This setting applies to every emulator that you start from that shell.
EMULATOR_TELEMETRY accepts on, true, or 1 to turn telemetry on, and off, false, or 0 to turn it off. Values aren’t case sensitive. Any other value turns telemetry off, and the startup notice shows a warning.
export EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off
aws-emulator
To turn telemetry off for every run on a machine, add these lines to the emulator settings file, config.toml. The file is ~/.aws/emulator/config.toml on Linux and macOS, and %USERPROFILE%\.aws\emulator\config.toml on Windows. To use a different file, set the EMULATOR_CONFIG environment variable to its path.
[telemetry]
enabled = false
In embedded mode, turn off telemetry in the options that you pass when you create the emulator.
use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions, Telemetry};
fn main() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default().telemetry(Telemetry::Off));
    let _http_client = emulator.http_client();
}
You might build a tool that includes the emulator, such as a test framework that other people run. If you do, tell your users about telemetry and give them a way to turn it off. You can also ship your tool with telemetry off.
Report bugs and fidelity gaps in GitHub Issues. The most useful report names the service, the operation, your SDK and version, the request you sent, and how the response differed from real AWS. This repository does not take PRs.
This software is licensed under the CC0 1.0 Universal (CC0-1.0) License, except the code in the vendor/ directory, which is under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE for details, and vendor/README.md for the license of the code in vendor/.

Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
18:13:52 UTC
03:13:52 KST

Gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms are facing a fresh wave of sweeping European Union rules that aim to make “your online experience fairer.” The newly proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) published by the EU Commission on Wednesday is designed to tackle practices that exploit consumers into spending more of their time and money online, including misleading prices or availability, addictive design features like gaming loot boxes, undisclosed influencer marketing, and more.
Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
The proposed Digital Fairness Act seeks to bolster consumer protections for online users.
“The Act will protect consumers of all ages shopping and browsing for goods or services online,” the EU Commission said in a news bulletin. “It will also mean fairer competition for businesses, which are expecting to save EU consumers up to €13.7 billion ($15.1 billion) a year.”
Here’s an overview of what the DFA proposal includes:
- A ban on manipulative marketing practices and so-called “dark patterns” that push consumers into making decisions they might not otherwise make, such as fake claims about a product almost being sold out.
- A requirement to give consumers the choice to turn off addictive features, such as persistent prompts, endless scrolling, and autoplay of videos. Restrictions around addictive design also apply to “AI companions and general conversational chatbots.”
- Restrictions on unfair practices that encourage overspending, such as banning gambling-like features (pay-to-win and pay-to-progress, for example) for minors.
- Requiring influencers to clearly disclose advertising content, and restrictions to prevent them from exploiting the trust of children.
- Restrictions on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive data.
- Making subscriptions and digital contracts easier to cancel, with prompts to remind customers about upcoming automatic renewals and free trial periods coming to an end.
- Requiring clear and transparent pricing, especially around dynamic pricing and purchases using virtual in-app currency. When consumers wait in virtual queues for cultural and sports event tickets, companies will have to show the current price in real time and at the highest possible price.
- Giving consumers the right to communicate with a human customer service representative, and clear rights using an AI agent to make purchases.
The scope of the restrictions being proposed is broad, and could have a significant impact on major parts of the online digital landscape, from the “rabbit hole” algorithms across YouTube, TikTok, and Meta platforms, to AI chatbots and apps like DuoLingo that relentlessly nudge users to keep interacting with them. Some gaming organizations have already slammed the DFA proposal, describing its restrictions around virtual currencies, loot boxes, and offering micro-transactions to minors as being “unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.”
Given this is a draft proposal, the DFA will undergo various approvals through the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union before being passed into law, and its current measures could be changed or removed entirely as part of that process. When (or if) it does come into force, the EU Commission says companies who violate the regulations could see fines of up to six percent of their worldwide annual turnover.
“Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services - not on their ability to exploit consumers or evade the rules. We are not making it harder to do business. We are making it harder to do business unfairly,” EU Commissioner Michael McGrath said in remarks following the DFA draft publication. “We cannot have 21st-century consumers protected by rules that have not kept pace with the 21st-century economy.”

Logitech Giving All 7,000 Employees the Day Off to Play GTA 6 (tomshardware.com) 34
			
		 	
				Under a new "Logi Game Day" initiative, Logitech is giving all 7,000 of its employees an extra paid day off to play GTA 6 when it launches on November 19. Employees and interns can use the day off anytime over the next year. Tom's Hardware reports:  As for Logitech, the company believes that it's time for people to move away from the belief that playing games is a waste of time, hence its new initiative. It makes sense for a company that makes gaming accessories to say that, of course, but CEO Hanneke Faber argues that the company sees "how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other." The hope will be that, by allowing employees to play games, a productivity boost will follow.

I Never Make Stuffing in the Oven — This Easy Recipe Is a Lifesaver for Thanksgiving

I Never Make Stuffing in the Oven — This Easy Recipe Is a Lifesaver for Thanksgiving
Thanksgiving is one of my favorite holidays. And as a vegetarian, it’s really all about the sides for me — my plate simply isn’t complete without a hefty scoop of stuffing. If you’re the one in charge of preparing the meal (hats off to you), you know that oven space comes at a premium on the big day. Well, thankfully this recipe might just give you a little of it back. With a bit of prep, your stuffing will be ready in a few hours of fully hands-off cooking — and then you can get on to making the other elements of the meal. Here’s why you should totally give it a try this Thanksgiving.
Get the recipe: Slow Cooker Stuffing
What Makes Slow Cooker Stuffing So Good
The hardest part of this recipe is making the croutons — seriously. To start, you’ll toast cubes of crusty bread for about an hour-and-a-half, checking and tossing them periodically until they’re crisp. But after that, it’s smooth sailing. Simply sauté the rest of the ingredients and seasonings, toss them with croutons and an eggy broth mixture, and let the slow cooker do its thing. In about 3 to 4 hours, you’ll have a delicious stuffing with incredible texture — all without even turning on the oven!
The pieces that are closer to the center are softer and more pillowy, while the outer chunks of bread have that crispy, chewy texture that I can’t get enough of. Plus, it’s soaked up all the delicious flavors of the broth, onion, celery, garlic, thyme, and sage (anything with those two herbs practically screams fall to me). It’s much more flavorful than the bagged stuff, and doesn’t require too much extra effort. Plus, you’ll be so thankful for the extra oven space for the candied yams, mac and cheese, and turkey on the big day.
How to Make Slow Cooker Stuffing
- Make the croutons. Toast the cubed bread until crispy.
- Sauté the vegetables. Cook the onion, celery, and garlic in melted butter, stirring in the thyme and sage at the end.
- Mix the stuffing. Whisk eggs, broth, salt, and pepper together. Add in the toasted bread and sautéed vegetables, and mix until combined.
- Slow-cook the stuffing. Add the mixture to a slow cooker and cook on low for about 3 to 4 hours.
Tips for Making Slow Cooker Stuffing
- Use stale bread: Stuffing is one of those recipes that’s pretty forgiving, and stale bread actually works perfectly here because it’s already dried-out, so you can skip the toasting step.
- Tweak to your liking: This recipe is pretty classic, but feel free to add your own spin with dried fruit, sausage, chestnuts, or mushrooms.
Get the recipe: Slow Cooker Stuffing

The Power and Legacy of Virginia Tech's Mac-Based Supercomputers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
17:30:47 UTC
02:30:47 KST

When we think about data centers today, we often picture rows of GPU-packed racks run by companies like Microsoft, Google, Amazon, and Meta, and used by AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Much of that hardware does one of two jobs: training new models or running finished ones to answer requests from millions of people around the world.
A supercomputer is built from many of the same parts but for a different purpose. It is typically owned by a government lab or university and designed for scientific simulation, such as modeling climate, nuclear physics, or new materials. That work demands high-precision math and very fast communication between processors. Rather than serving the masses, a supercomputer is shared among researchers, whose large jobs wait in a queue and run according to a schedule.
Early examples like UNIVAC and the IBM 7030 were used by scientists working on atomic research. The Cray-1 came along in the mid-70s and accelerated such work to new levels. Each of these machines brought with it new technologies that made those breakthroughs possible. They were also fairly bespoke, built of components regular nerds could only dream about.
Over time, that changed. By the time the 1990s rolled around, companies like Cray saw their hardware being outpaced by newcomers who were packing far more processors into their products. The kicker? Those processors were much more pedestrian than the custom silicon older supercomputers were built around.
In 1998, David Bader built what he calls “the first bona fide Linux supercomputer” with off-the-shelf parts, including the Intel Pentium II.1
That brings us to 2003, and the subject of today’s article: Virginia Tech’s Mac-based supercomputers.
Bang for the Buck
As you can see from these photos, System X — pronounced “System Ten”2 — was built with 1,100 Power Mac G5s:
Photos from Virginia Tech’s Advanced Research Computing website, via the Wayback Machine.
Honestly, I could end this article right here. Look how badass this all is! I really do love the look of the Power Mac G5.
Virginia Tech built this supercomputer in the summer of 2003, with the goal of hitting 10 teraflops. Once it was up and running that fall, it ranked as the world’s third-fastest computer, and the fastest at an academic institution. You can see from this video that the G5 was chosen to hit these numbers without breaking the bank:
(This video played as part of Apple’s product introduction for the Power Mac G5 itself.)
The total cost was $5.2 million,3 a far cry from the $400 million spent to build the fastest supercomputer at the time, the Earth Simulator.
(System X also looked much cooler.)
Both Virginia Tech faculty members and students could get time on the machine free of charge, and thanks to the dual 2.0 GHz processors inside each G5, their projects could tap into vast resources easily.
On the software front, every node ran Mac OS X. The machines arrived running Mac OS X 10.2.7, with plans to move to Panther shortly after.
Each G5 came equipped with 4 GB of DDR400 RAM, a 160 GB Serial ATA hard drive, and a Mellanox InfiniBand PCI-X card, which allowed the machines to be linked to each other and to the network over high-speed cables. Notably, the Power Mac G5 didn’t support ECC memory. That would matter later.
The G5s were unboxed and installed by students and faculty:
The whole thing came together pretty quickly, according to this FAQ:
Planning began in January of 2003. Facilities planning began in April of 2003. Renovations began the first week of August and were completed on September 23, 2003. Computers, network equipment, and cables began arriving the first week of September 2003. The computers arrived in six shipments during a seven day period and were processed into the racks in less than 2 hours per shipment with no more than 30 volunteers working a shift.
Ethernet cabling (roughly 1200 connections) was done by a four man team from our internal communications and network services group and was completed in less than 14 days.
InfiniBand cabling (roughly 1700 connections) began September 13, 2003 and was completed by a team of five people in 10 days.
I was lucky to get an email about this from Sam Davies, who was a student and an Apple Campus Representative at Virginia Tech at the time. He told me:
In the summer of 2003, I was fortunate to be a part of the team working to put System X together (that was the official name, unofficially the Mac community and everyone else called it “Big Mac”).
The first 1,100 G5s off of Apple’s assembly line were unloaded from trucks, unboxed, and carried into server racks by a huge team of faculty, staff, Apple project folks, and student volunteers like me. Only one G5 tower in the batch of 1100 couldn’t be used, and that was because one of the Apple sales reps dropped it. (Those handles are sharp!)
Of course, having a bunch of tower machines stuffed into racks isn’t very space-efficient. The next year, Apple had a solution.
The Xserve G5
Here’s Apple PR, in January 2004:
Apple today introduced Xserve G5, the most powerful Xserve yet, delivering over 30 gigaflops of processing power per system, about 60 percent more than the PowerPC G4-based Xserve. Xserve G5 features the same revolutionary PowerPC G5, 64-bit processor used in Virginia Tech’s cluster of Power Mac G5s—the world’s third fastest supercomputer. With unparalleled performance and manageability in a 1U rack-mount enclosure, Xserve G5 is the perfect server for today’s UNIX-based applications.
Xserve G5 includes a new system controller with up to 8GB of PC3200 error correcting code (ECC) memory; three hot-plug Serial ATA drive modules that deliver up to 750GB of storage; optional internal hardware RAID; dual PCI-X slots, supporting 133 MHz PCI-X cards with over 1 GBps of throughput; and dual on-board Gigabit Ethernet for high-performance networking.
The press release continues:
“Xserve G5 delivers just what our customers have been asking for,” said Philip Schiller, Apple’s senior vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With dual G5 processing power and up to 8GB of ECC memory, Xserve G5 is affordable, easy to manage and easy to cluster. Starting as low as $2,999, no one can offer better price performance in a 1U rack-mount design.”
Available with either single or dual 2.0 GHz PowerPC G5 processors, the Xserve G5 architecture is based on an execution core that features massively parallel computation for an unprecedented 215 in-flight instructions, full symmetric multi-processing, two double precision floating-point units and an optimized Velocity Engine. Xserve G5 has the industry’s fastest front side processor bus—running at up to 1.0 GHz and delivering 8 GBps per processor.
Building on the engineering feats first introduced in the Power Mac G5, Xserve G5 squeezes the incredible performance of dual PowerPC G5 processors into an ultra-thin 1U enclosure. An innovative copper heat sink design effectively removes heat from the processors while eight high-performance fans provide airflow for cooling the system. The fans are individually managed and monitored by a dedicated fan control processor; if a single fan fails the others speed up to compensate. The 1U enclosure has an array of over 30 sensors, including eight dedicated to temperature control, that continually monitor all critical system functions throughout the server.
Tech tore down the Power Mac version of System X in January 2004 and rebuilt it with Xserve G5s that summer. ECC memory was a big part of the reason. As the school put it: “We needed to upgrade the system to something with error correcting code (ECC) RAM. The Power Macs did not support it and the XServes were coming.”
The new array was made up of 1,100 dual 2.3 GHz Xserve G5 servers and six Xserve RAIDs. Those 2.3 GHz machines were custom-built by Apple for Virginia Tech; the public wouldn’t be able to buy one until January 2005. Each one had 4 GB of that sweet, sweet ECC RAM and an 80 GB Serial ATA drive.
The installation photos really show the difference between the G5 towers and G5 servers when it comes to density:
The aforementioned FAQ sheds some light on this version of System X:
The initial machine was torn down by eight people between January 14 and January 19, 2004.
The Xserve upgrade was completed by a team of Virginia Tech and Apple volunteers over a much more staggered period of time. Rack preparation and pre-cabling of Ethernet began in February and was completed by less than ten people.
Machines arrived in odd batches beginning in the middle of June 2004 and were processed into the racks by no more than 16 people working for no more than 9 hours a shift (first shipment; 304 Xserves racked in 9 hours by a 16 person team).
Final cabling was completed over a two-week period by no more than ten people working a shift. The machine was back online for benchmarking by August 1, 2004.
The new hardware pushed System X to 12.25 teraflops. The school boasted that “the upgraded version was #7 in the 2004 TOP500 list, and cost one-fifth as much as the second least-expensive system in the top 10.”
Apple boasted about it as well, profiling the machine on its website:
Virginia Tech gained international honors for building the fastest supercomputer at any academic institution in the world. And they did it using Power Mac G5s. From that milestone, Virginia Tech has moved ahead again with System X, a new cluster using 1,100 Xserve G5s.
[…]
“When we built the first supercomputer from Power Mac G5s, we proved that a radically-different communications technology could be used to create a large-scale computing platform,” says Dr. Srinidhi Varadarajan, director of the university’s Terascale Computing Facility and the system’s lead designer.
“We’re recognized for knowing how to build these terascale computing machines — and with very good price performance.
“But the measure of the facility is the kind of science it produces.”
Varadarajan later became CTO of AppAssure, a backup software company that Dell acquired in 2012. May we all be as cool as him one day:
Tech Goes Intel
By the middle of 2007, System X had slipped to 71st place on the TOP500 list, but was still serving the community in and around Tech.
In November 2008, its younger sibling System G was brought online. Firmly in the Intel era, System G was made up of 324 Mac Pros,4 each with two 4-core 2.8 GHz Intel Xeon processors (for a total of 2,592 processor cores) and 8 GB of RAM.
It debuted at #280 on the November 2008 TOP500 list with a Linpack score of 16.87 teraflops, though Virginia Tech claimed 22.8 teraflops of sustained performance.
Chris Foresman wrote about the supercomputer for Ars Technica:
Virginia Tech’s Center for High-End Computing System [sic] (CHECS) is famous for building a 1100-node, G5-based supercomputing cluster in 2003 called System X. At the time it was built, it ranked as the third fastest supercomputer in the world with a sustained performance of just over 12 teraflops. The CHECS is building a new cluster, this time using 324 Mac Pro towers, that will have a theoretical computing capacity of 29 teraflops.
The new system will not replace System X, according to CHECS Director Dr. Srinidhi Varadarajan. “Unlike System X, which is a production machine for computational science and engineering researchers, the new system is intended to be pure computer science research system,” he told Ars. The system will be used to study two main areas: power-aware software systems that can adjust performance automatically to maximize efficiency, and distributed shared memory systems that can run existing threaded code on high-performance clusters “as if they were scaled up versions of multi-core desktops.”
The article continues and explains why the Intel Xserve wasn’t chosen for the new array:
Varadarajan and his team chose Mac Pros for a few reasons. For one, Xserves are power dense, which requires a lot of cooling to prevent thermal hot spots. “System X has a hybrid liquid-air cooling system in a dedicated facility, which enables significantly better cooling without hot spots. This machine is however, housed in a conventional air cooled room,” Varadarajan told us. Also, the Mac Pro has a large number of power and temperature sensors built in, which is necessary for the power/performance research and tuning, as well as an additional full-height PCI Express 2.0 slot for use in other research projects. And, despite common wisdom to the contrary, the Mac Pros beat other systems on price. “The Mac Pros are highly competitive even against building a white box off the cheapest prices,” he added.
System G was designed to be as power-efficient as possible. Here’s a bit from an old CHECS website:
The system is the first supercomputer running over quad data rate (QDR) InfiniBand (40Gbs) interconnect technology. System G (for “green”) also has unique power-aware capabilities, with thousands of power and thermal sensors allowing CHECS researchers to design and develop algorithms and systems software that achieve high-performance with modest power requirements, and to test such systems at unprecedented scale. With a sustained (Linpack) performance of 22.8 TFlops, System G is the largest power-aware research system and one of the largest computer science systems research clusters in the world.
This VT Magazine article has more:
“It’s twice as powerful, a third the size, and uses a third of the power,” says Kirk W. Cameron, associate professor of computer science in the College of Engineering. Cameron helped build G with Srinidhi Varadarajan, associate professor of computer science and director of the Center for High-End Computing Systems.
Unlike System X, System G was created to improve system design first and foremost and to be used as a production computer second. The $1.2 million machine was built to develop new, high-performance software tools and applications with paramount efficiency.
When Cameron and Varadarajan, assisted by a team of fellow faculty members and scores of graduate students, set out to build G, they had an end-goal in mind. They wanted G to not only be fast but also environmentally friendly. Hence the “G” for green. When Cameron arrived at Virginia Tech in 2004–on the heels of X’s opening, and attracted to Tech because of X–“green computing” wasn’t even an industry catchphrase. But Cameron already was looking ahead at the need to conserve power.
He previously worked for Los Alamos National Laboratory, handling performance duties, “squeezing as much power as possible” out of the facilities’ supercomputers, he says. This was in 2002, well before the recent call to arms in green energy. G went on-line in 2008. “Now everybody says they are doing it, but we were lucky enough to have done it first,” Cameron says.
The system is stocked with advanced power-management capabilities, such as power-aware central processing units (CPUs), disks, and memory. A network of advanced power and thermal sensors runs throughout the entire system, with Cameron and Varadarajan able to track how much power each CPU unit in each Apple tower is using.
Using power caps, the system is able to run on lower steam when not in use or in partial use, as opposed to older supercomputer systems that run at full blast, needlessly using power, on a continuous basis. Temperature control is carefully monitored as to not overuse the massive air-conditioning units that keep the stacked, side-by-side computers from overheating.
“We wanted to try and find the most efficient way to use computers,” says Cameron.
While System X served researchers across the university and was eventually run by Virginia Tech’s Advanced Research Computing division, System G was a computer science research machine. It belonged to CHECS, was sponsored in part by the National Science Foundation (NSF), and was housed on the campus of VT’s Corporate Research Center.
That makes finding additional details about System G tricky. Even locating photos of the array proved futile; the ones Virginia Tech published in 2008 have vanished from the web.
That’s when Dr. Cameron answered an email I had sent him, asking about System G and, if possible, for any photos he had of the Mac Pros. He graciously replied with first-hand information about the project, including a couple of incredibly rare photos:
These are the only images of System G I have seen, and I cannot imagine how amazing this must have been in person.
They also prove yet again that guys with racks and racks of Mac hardware are just much cooler than the rest of us:
He also provided insight into how the project was designed to make it easier to capture and analyze huge amounts of data. The team captured data from the Mac Pros’ built-in temperature sensors, recorded the voltage and current going into the racks, and logged environmental data from the room itself.
All of this data was synthesized into human-readable information that helped inform their research and keep System G as efficient as possible:
The Legacies of System X & System G
Both systems are now gone, but their legacy remains. Choosing Mac hardware to build a supercomputer isn’t the status quo, but the work of Varadarajan, Cameron, and others proved it could be done, and on a budget.
System X may be the most famous Mac-based supercomputer, but it wasn’t the only one. In January 2005, Bowie State University in Maryland unveiled XSEED, a $1 million array of 224 Xserve G5s. In the same timeframe, the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign launched its Turing Xserve Cluster, made up of 640 dual-processor 2.0 GHz Xserve G5s. The University of California, Los Angeles had Dawson, which started as an array of 128 Xserve G5s.
System G’s legacy includes its focus on power usage, under the direction of Dr. Cameron. His work has centered on the power consumption of high-performance computing systems since the early 2000s. He is a founding member of SPECpower, helped create the Green500 list, and has worked to steer the supercomputer industry toward treating performance per watt as an important metric when architecting systems.
He is still a faculty member at Virginia Tech today.
My research into System X started in July, and what was going to be a simple blog post turned into something much bigger and much more special. I had no idea System G existed when I started this, and I am thrilled I could help tell its story. My thanks to everyone who helped make this article possible, including Dr. Cameron, Sam Davies, Casey Liss, Jason Snell, and others.
- NASA’s Beowulf project had strung together commodity PCs running Linux as early as 1994. ↩︎
- According to Virginia Tech, the “X” stood for the original goal of 10 teraflops of operating speed, not for Mac OS X. ↩︎
- That’s the figure Virginia Tech used in 2003. A later version of the school’s FAQ put the machine at $5.7 million, plus $2 million to renovate the facility that housed it. ↩︎
- Some Virginia Tech sources, including VT Magazine and the school’s press release, put the count at 325. In reviewing first-hand documentation of System G (more on that in a moment), I can confidently say the array was made up of 324 machines. ↩︎

FAQ
Can the integration log into sites and act behind a login?
Yes. Integrations authenticate into portals, dashboards, and internal tools to read data and take actions.
Do I need to store my credentials?
No. You can use Pomerado without storing any credentials: simply pass any needed logins with your API request. For convenience, we also offer secure credential storage, including 2FA. Note: Pomerado securely retains hashes of sign-in identifiers to enforce single-login limits per website.
What about captchas, rate limits, and getting blocked?
We natively enforce rate limits and handle anti-bot measures (e.g., with residential proxies) to protect customers from those risks.
What data does Pomerado retain?
We only persist data necessary to keep the API working for a particular site. Task results are erased once delivered, or within 60 minutes if never read, and credentials are stored only if you choose to save them.
How do you handle PII and sensitive information?
We use state of the art models to redact and strip out PII, so sensitive details aren't kept once your task is done.
What do we need to get started?
Create an account and connect to the Pomerado API or MCP.
Contact us
Whether you are sharpening a personal assistant, automating a legacy process, or streamlining an internal workflow, Pomerado can accelerate you and your team.

Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
17:09:58 UTC
02:09:58 KST

Toyota is dusting off the Scion badge for a radically different mission. Rather than targeting youth-market hatchbacks, “Scion by Toyota” is being positioned as an experimental mobility incubator — and its first vehicle is an authentic Japanese-style kei truck built in Indiana.
Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
Toyota is reviving the Scion badge as an experimental mobility incubator—starting with an Indiana-built, 25-mph kei truck engineered for American fleets.
Kei vehicles, which are built to satisfy Japan’s light vehicle regulations, are enjoying surging popularity around the world, including here in the US. More than 30,000 used kei trucks have been imported into the US since 2020, with roughly 7,500 units entering the country each year. Even President Trump is a fan, telling reporters last year that he authorized the Department of Transportation to approve their production.
Toyota looks to be the first to test the American market’s appetite for the tiny trucks. The choice to use the Scion brand, which was discontinued in 2016, would seem to indicate that the automaker is hoping to appeal to younger car buyers. But more than that, Toyota says it sees Scion as a testing ground for utility, outdoor adventure, and customization that wouldn’t typically fit in any of its other models.
When it lands in the second half of 2027, Scion’s KEI-01 sports a 660cc three-cylinder gas engine paired with a continuously variable transmission. It won’t win any drag races, but it should delivery enough power for stop-and-go driving while using a minimum amount of fuel.
It’s true super power comes from its diminutive dimensions. At roughly 11 feet long and under 5 feet wide, the KEI-01 is about half the footprint of a full-size pickup. It can easily thread through cramped alleys, narrow barn aisles, garden gates, or busy campus pathways where standard trucks can’t fit.
The truck features an on-demand 4WD system with a push-button locking mode. If you’re cutting across muddy farm turf, gravel work paths, or wet slush, power splits to all four wheels to keep the truck from spinning out or getting stuck.
Inside, the vehicle looks pretty cheap, with lots of black plastic and a noticeable absence of any premium materials. That will hopefully help keep the price nice and low — though Toyota hasn’t disclosed any trim options yet. Japanese imports typically range from $6,000 to $12,000.
Because it is certified under federal Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) rules — also used for golf carts and golf cart-adjacent vehicles — its top speed is strictly capped at 25 mph. The truck bed features three sides that fold completely flat, removing the need to lean over high-metal sides to drop in cargo. The KEI-01 can hold up to 600 pounds of soil, tools, or gear, and can easily tow small utility trailers or mowers.
Unlike an open utility cart or ATV, this tiny truck has a fully sealed cabin equipped with both heating and air conditioning. The extended roofline gives drivers extra headroom, reclining seats, and interior storage behind the seats to keep tools dry and secure. True to classic Japanese utility imports, the steering wheel is on the right side of the cab. Beyond the cool factor, curbside delivery and stepping directly onto sidewalks or worksite shoulders is quicker and safer.
To make the KEI-01 to conform to the rules and regs of auto manufacturing in the US, Toyota is investing $34 million into its Princeton, Indiana manufacturing plant to stand up local assembly and add roughly 50 jobs. Production kicks off in the second half of 2027, but everyday drivers won’t be able to buy one off the lot immediately.
Scion by Toyota is launching the mini-truck strictly as a fleet-focused pilot program targeting corporate campuses, farms, municipalities, and local delivery operators, distributed through a specialized group of existing Toyota dealerships. While Toyota notes it may consider opening up sales to consumer retail down the road if demand justifies it, the initial rollout is very much treated as an experiment to evaluate real-world US utility.
The KEI-01 was joined by two adventure-themed concepts that show Scion’s new focus extends far beyond budget hatchbacks. The SxS Concept packs a 300-plus-horsepower hybrid turbo setup for high-speed off-roading, while the modular BKE Concept explores compact personal mobility. Together, they signal that Scion’s second act is aimed squarely at niche utility and experimental recreation.
Images by Toyota
