The Computer Graphics Book Of Knowledge
History of Computer Graphics (CG)
Computer Graphics (CG) was first created as a 
visualization tool for scientists and engineers in government 
and corporate research centers such as Bell Labs and Boeing 
in the 1950s. Later the tools would be developed at 
Universities in the 60s and 70s at places such as Ohio State 
University, MIT, University of Utah, Cornell, North Carolina 
and the New York Institute of Technology.	
The early breakthroughs that took place in academic 
centers continued at research centers such as the famous 
Xerox PARC in the 1970ąs. These efforts broke first into 
broadcast video graphics and then major motion pictures in 
the late 70ąs and early 1980ąs. Computer graphic research 
continues today around the world, now joined by the research 
and development departments of entertainment and production 
companies. Companies such as George Lucasąs Industrial 
Light and Magic are constantly redefining the cutting edge 
of computer graphic technology in order to present the world 
with a new synthetic digital reality.
1940s
	The very first łcomputer assisted˛ graphics began in 
many different unrelated fields around the world. There is a 
very blurred line that is crossed somewhere between 
mechanical and analog computer assisted graphics, and the 
first directly digital computer generated graphics that would 
associate with today as being true łCG˛.
The very first radiosity image. 
While at MIT in the 1940s, Professors Parry Moon and 
Domina Eberle Spencer were using their field of applied 
mathematics to calculate highly accurate global lighting 
models which they called łinterflection reflection˛. The 
illumination algorithms were based on those by H. H. Higbie, 
published in his 1934 book, Lighting Calculations.
Lacking any display or output mechanism, the image 
itself was created by painstakingly selecting Munsel paper 
samples that matched the output data of their mathematical 
model. The paper was cut out and ironed together by hand to 
create the image shown here in print for the first time in 
over 50 years.
	[IMAGE OF THE RADIOSITY PIC]
(The original image is still hanging in the office of 
Dr. Domina Spencer at the University of Connecticut.)
The images were first presented at the 1946 National 
Technical Conference of the Illuminating Engineering Society 
of North America, and published two years later (in color) in 
the book: Lighting Design by Moon, P., and D. E. Spencer. 
1948. (Addison-Wesley. Cambridge, MA) The book was used for 
many years to teach lighting theory at MIT in the 
architecture curriculum there. Dr. Spencer went on to teach 
at Tufts, Brown, Rhode Island School of Design, and the 
University of Connecticut where she remains active today.
1950s
 €John Whitney Sr. devises his own computer assisted 
mechanisms to create some of his graphic artwork and short 
films. One of his sons John Jr. works with and learns from 
his father from childhood through high school.see biography
€Pioneering artists Stan VanderBeck, Michael Noll and 
others at Bell Labs in New Jersey created computer assisted 
graphics using analog computer devices and plotter output. 
Later, in the mid 1960s, digital computers and film recorders 
would be used to produce some of the earliest CG animated 
films
€Bill Fetter experimented with early vector graphic CAD 
at Boeing (Seattle) in the late l950s using an IBM 7094 
computer with punch card input and a Gerber plotter. 
1950 
Artist Ben Laposky uses analog computers to help him create 
oscilloscope artwork.
1951
Vectorscope-type graphics display on the Whirlwind computer 
at MIT. A device similar to a light pen allowed direct input 
to the screen.
The General Motors Research Laboratory begins to study 
the role of computer aided graphical design applications. 
(This would later result in the development of the DAC-1)
1955
SAGE system at MITs Lincoln Lab uses the first true light pen 
as input device. (Bert Sutherland) 
1956
Lawrence Livermore National Labs connects graphics 
display to IBM 704; use film recorder for color images
Bertram Herzog at the University of Michigan Computing 
Center uses analog computers to generate CRT graphic studies 
of military vehicle behavior.
1957
1st image-processed photo at National Bureau of Standards.
(By whom? Why?)
The IBM 740-780 (paired with a separate IBM 704 computer 
system) generated a sequence of points on a CRT in order to 
represent lines or shapes. Time lapse film photography was 
used to capture the images as they were drawn on the screen.
The Defence Departments Advanced Research Project Agency 
(ARPA) is founded.
1958
	MITąs Lincoln Labs: Funded in part by the Air Force; 
Steven Coons, Ivan Sutherland, and Timothy Johnson begin 
working with the TX-2 computer system to manipulate drawn 
pictures. Ivan Sutherland later began refining the work into 
his famous Sketchpad system while a student at MIT. DEC 
later commercialized the TX-2 as the PDP-6.
1959
The first commercial film recorder  the General Dynamics 
Stromberg Carlson 4020. (Produced in San Diego, CA.)
1959
DAC-1 (Design Augmented by Computers): First computer aided 
drawing system. Created by Don Hart and Ed Jacks at General 
Motors Research Laboratory and IBM. (Not unveiled until 
the Fall Joint Computer Conference in Detroit in 1964.) The 
system was originally based upon a IBM 7090 computer (later 
upgraded to a 7094 in 1963) augmented with extra disc space 
and a specially designed IBM 7969 łimage processing system˛. 
Input was with punch cards, but was also capable of scanning 
in drawings. The final data could be output to either 35mm 
film (by way of a CRT), a hard copy plotter, or used to drive 
computer controlled machining devices.
Biography: John Whitney Sr. (1917-1995) 
A Los Angeles native, Whitney was a pioneer in many 
forms of experimental and abstract art before turning to 
computers to aid in his graphic creations. He attended Pomona 
College in California in the 1940's and was the first in a 
wave of artists to begin new techniques of computer 
assisted graphics. 
The integration of analog computer controlled camera and 
artwork were at first more a pioneering use of motion control 
than of computer graphics. In point of fact, the devices 
these early artists used were not even thought of as 
computers, being more akin to analog music synthesizers. From 
his experience working in the aircraft industry during World 
War II, Whitney realized that components of a computerized 
anti-aircraft controller could be used to drive his 
mechanisms. One of his sons (John Jr.), recalled buying the 
łstate-of-the-art˛ M7 anti-aircraft control computer at 
surplus. The still unopened crate was 12 feet long, 7 feet 
wide and seven feet tall. These synchronized mechanisms would 
ultimately be used to calculate abstract shapes, and change 
them over time to create beautifully abstract forms and 
animation.
In the 1950ąs Whitney worked in Hollywood as an 
animation director at UPA, most notably contributing graphic 
elements for the Saul Bass designed opening credits to 
Hitchcockąs łVertigo˛. Whitney then founded Motion Graphics 
Inc. in 1960 and produced animation for both television and 
film, devising the łslit scan˛ technique for his early short 
film łLapis˛. This technique would later be made famous when 
used by Con Pederson as a portion of the famous łStarGate˛ 
ending sequence of Stanley Kubrickąs ł2001: A Space Odyssey˛.
In 1966 with the help of a grant from IBM and a Fortran 
programmer named Jack Citron(sp?), Whitney made his first 
digital computer short film called "Permutations". His next 
works: Matrix 1 and Matrix 2 were done at Cal Tech, 
followed by Matrix 3 at Triple-I in 1971. It was at this 
time that he met Larry Cuba who would later be asked by 
Whitney to collaborate with him in 1975 on his last 16mm film 
project łArabesque˛, funded in part by an NEA grant. Both 
Whitney and Cuba would work briefly at Robert Abeląs effects 
company before digital computer graphics were begun there.
Beginning in the mid 1980's, a new collaborator Jerry 
Reed(sp?) translated Cubaąs Fortran code into Pascal for use 
on new personal computer hardware that Whitney could use at 
home. Whitney continued to create abstract computer animation 
on his own with the aid of this new PC technology that freed 
him from the reliance of large company owned mainframe 
machines and the need for sponsored grants. His work would be 
displayed in galleries on the same PC hardware he created it 
on. His last commercially available collection of works, 
called łMoondrum˛ was released on video in the late 1980ąs.
Today his son Michael Whitney is serving as archiver for his 
fathers work, and recently organized a retrospective showing 
at UCLA.
1960's
€łComputer assisted graphics˛ were being created more 
widely as a new and unique art-form by people such as Charles 
Csuri, Ken Knowlton and John Whitley Sr.
€Many pioneering artistic films and artworks were 
created at Bell Labs from about 1962 to 1967 by artists and 
programmers such as E.E.Zajac, Leon D. Harmon, Ken Knowlton, 
A.Michael Noll, Lilian Shwartz, M.R. Schroeder and Stan 
Vanderbeek. An IBM 7094 computer ran a Stromberg-Calson 4020 
film recorder, programmed in FORTRAN to run Ken Knowltons 
Beflix animation system. 
Much of the nation-wide university computer science 
research conducted at the time was due in part to funding 
from the governmentąs "Advanced Research Project Agency" 
(ARPA). ARPA at the time took a very hands-off approach to 
funding. This allowed researchers an un-pressured environment 
in which to concentrate on the work, without the heavy 
bureaucracy, paperwork and political constraints more common 
today. Much to the benefit of researches was Ivan Sutherland 
who headed ARPA for a time. With good funding, little 
oversight and many brilliant young minds inspiring each 
other, it was a unique and special time that produced the 
very foundation of todayąs computer graphic tool sets.
€Herb Freeman had a school of CG development going on 
at NYU including Alvy Ray Smith in his first professor's job 
out of Stanford in 1969. Freeman and his students had already 
solved the hidden-line problem, a very big deal at the time.
[Quote] łAlso on the pixel side of things, Azriel 
Rosenfeld at the Univ of MD, and Ron Baecker was developing 
some of the very first computer animation. I saw his system 
GENESYS at an NYU demo in the early 1970s which means Ron 
probably did the development (in Canada, Toronto, I think) in 
the late 1960s.˛ -Alvy Ray Smith
€Nicholas Negroponte teaches Computer Aided Design 
(CAD) at M.I.T in the mid to late 60s, and develops the 
URBAN5 system. A light pen allows interaction directly on the 
CRT, in combination with keyboard instructions. Points and 
symbols are added in orthographic mode with a perspective 
option entered after the fact in order to view structures 
three-dimensionally. An łintelligent˛ system study, URBAN5 
was abandoned by 1968 in favor of other projects.
€łThe Society for Information Displays˛ is formed 
in the early 60s, publishing papers dealing mostly with 
military applications.
	€At this same time, practical commercial and industrial 
use of computer graphics begins to take hold in many areas of 
design and manufacturing. Throughout the decade at Boeing, 
William Fetter and Robert Woodruff (Computing Technology 
Administrator) leads many important industrial applications 
of vector generated CG. 
€Architectural and urban planning programs (typically 
written in FORTRAN on machines like the IBM 1130 or 1800) are 
used at the firm łSkidmore, Owings & Merrill˛ in Chicago and 
in the University of Texas School of Architecture. A sample 
workstation would consist of a Rand tablet providing input, 
with output to pen plotters such as the Calcomp.
€In the late 60s, the Electronics Laboratory of 
General Electric (Syracuse, NY) produces a prototype 
visualization system for NASA and the Office of Naval 
Research. The system produced real-time color raster graphics 
on a monitor as a training aid to astronauts going to land on 
the moon. This same system was used by Prof. Peter Kamnitzer 
of the UCLA School of Architecture and Urban Planning to 
simulate urban development plans.  
Biography: Dr. Dave C. Evans (1924-1998) MORE
One of a very few who could be called a true "founding 
father" of computer graphics, Dave Evans is perhaps best know 
for being the co-founder of "Evans & Sutherland Computer 
Corporation". Mr. Evans was at one time chairman of the 
computer science departments at both the University of 
California Berkeley and University of Utah, where he started 
the venerable doctoral program that would give birth to so 
much of the foundation of our industry. Evans first 
associated with Ivan Sutherland at both Berkeley and the 
Pentagon's "Advanced Research Project Agency" (ARPA). 
Mr. Evans made many contributions to a wide range of 
computer technologies, and a great many of his students went 
on to flourish in the brand new field of computer graphics, 
becoming true pioneers themselves. Students of Mr. Evans 
include Alan Kay(Co-founder of Xerox PARC), Jim Clark 
(founder of both Silicon Graphics and Co-founder of Netscape 
Communications), John Warnock(Co-founder of Adobe Systems) 
and Edwin Catmull(see biography in Programming chapter).
Dave Evans passed away on Oct.3rd, 1998.
 
1960
William Fetter of Boeing coins the term "computer 
graphics" for his human factors cockpit drawings. With help 
from Walter Bernhardt, and others, Fetter input an aircraft 
drawingąs coordinates into a database and plotted out a 
calculated perspective on a łIllustromat 1100˛ plotter.
John Whitney Sr. founds Motion Graphics, Inc. in LA.
1961/62 
Spacewar: The first popular computer graphic game 
written by students Steve Russell, Slug Russell, Shag Graetz, 
and Alan Kotok of MIT to run on the DEC PDP-1. (DEC's PDP-1 
cost $120,000 and MITąs was one of only 50 ever built) The 
large round CRT display featured graphics controlled by 
primitive handmade joysticks. The object being to maneuver 
away from a gravitational łsun˛ force at the center, and 
avoid the other enemy ships, while trying to blast him with 
your own space torpedoes! 
The original source code (which ran on 4k of memory!) 
can still be found at
www.media.mit.edu/groups/el/projects/spacewar/sources  
or ftp://ftp.digital.com/pub/DEC/sim/sources/sim_2.3d.tar.Z
There's also a copy of the PDP-1 manual at 
www.dbit.com/~greeng3/pdp1/pdp1.html 
1962
"Sketchpad: A Man-Machine Graphical Communication 
System"  is presented by Ivan Sutherland as his Ph.D. thesis 
at the M.I.T. Lincoln Laboratory. The user could input simple 
lines and curves by drawing directly on the screen with a 
light pen. The computer, the TX-2, had a whopping 320 
kilobytes of memory and a 9 inch monochromatic CRT.
	While Sketchpad was strictly 2D, a few years later 
Timothy Johnson expanded its capabilities into three 
dimensions as łSketchpad 3˛. The display CRT was divided up 
into the now familiar four views, top front side and 
perspective.
ARPA J.C.R. Licklider is put in charge of the new Information 
Processing Techniques Office (IPTO) at the Defense 
Departments Advanced Research Project Agency (APRA).
The initial $14 million dollar budget supported projects at 
MIT, Berkeley and Carnegie-Mellon. 
1963 
	Biography: Ivan Sutherland
Born in 1938, Hastings, Nebraska; Ivan Sutherland is truly an 
early łfounding father˛ of computer graphics. After 
completing his Ph.D. at M.I.T.(where he developed Sketchpad) 
in 1963, Ivan Sutherland joined the army and was assigned to 
the NSA as an electrical engineer. One year later, he was 
transferred to the Defense Department's Advanced Research 
Projects Agency (ARPA, later DARPA), and given responsibility 
for the newly-established Information Processing Techniques 
office. At age 26, Lt. Sutherland was given a secretary and 
$15 million a year, and was told to "go sponsor computer 
research." Which he gladly did for the following two years 
until joining the faculty at Harvard late in 1966. It was 
here with student Bob Sproull that they developed the Head 
Mounted Display (HUD), for remote viewing; the first 
łVirtual Reality˛. 
	In 1968 Ivan formed the Evans & Sutherland company 
with partner Dave Evans. Ivan was now a part time tenured 
professor at the University of Utah, where Evans was the 
founding head of the Computer Science Department. Dr. 
Sutherland had first met Evans during a visit to U.C. 
Berkeley as part of his ARPA work.
Ivan's last research in computer graphics was a paper 
titled: "A Characterization of Ten Hidden-Surface 
Algorithms," by Sutherland, Sproull and Schumacker. The paper 
solved many of the largest problems of the day in this 
critical area of rendering and display technology.
Later, as co-founder (with Carver Mead) and head of the 
Department of Computer Science at California Institute of 
Technology from 1976 - 1980, Dr. Sutherland developed and 
promoted courses involving integrated circuit design, the 
seed of knowledge that helped create the Silicon Valley 
industry.
In the early 1980s at Carnegie Mellon University, Ivan 
did some research on a six legged walking robot, large enough 
to carry a driver. (And controlled by a joy stick acquired by 
brother Bert from his contacts in the Navy as a former 
fighter pilot!)
In 1980, Ivan and Bob Sproull had started the consulting 
firm łSutherland, Sproull & Associates˛. Sun bought the 
company in 1990, which then became the nucleus of Sun 
Microsystems Laboratories.

Charles Csuri created an analogue computer and used it to

The 1st computer art competition, sponsored by Computers

1966 
"Odyssey":  The first consumer computer graphics games

Permutations: With a grant from IBM and a Fortran programmer 
named Jack Citron(sp?), John Whitney Sr. made the first 
digital computer short film. An IBM 2250 Graphic Display 
Console created dot patterns which were then recorded onto 
black and white 35mm film. The filmed images were then 
further enhanced with a specially designed optical printer to 
add secondary motion and color.
As Associate Professor at Harvard, Ivan Sutherland and his 
students, Bob Sproull, Jim Clark and others, took earlier 
"Remote Reality" vision systems of the Bell Helicopter 
project, and turned it into what we now call Virtual 
Reality by replacing the camera with computer images. The 
first such computer environment was no more than a wire-frame 
room with the cardinal directions -- North, South, East, and 
West initialed on the walls. The viewer could "enter" the 
room by way of the West door, and turn to look out windows in 
the other three directions. 
Affectionately called łThe Sword of Damocles˛ because of 
its ceiling mounted gear, what they called the "Head-
Mounted Display," later became known as Virtual Reality.
The International Conference on Design and Planning: 
łComputers in Design and Communication˛ is held at the 
University of Waterloo (Ontario). Organized by Professors 
Constant and Krampen of the Design Department, it was brought 
together to enlighten and inform designers of emerging 
computer technologies.
1967 
[QUOTE] łAt the same time that geometry-based computer 
graphics (CG) was being invented so was sampling theory-based 
computer graphics, often called image processing (IP) or 
imaging. In the early days, two conferences - one for each 
half of the discipline - would be held side by side. One of 
the earliest journals was called Journal of Computer 
Graphics and Image Processing. Its editors were Herb 
Freeman and Azriel Rosenfeld (CG and IP, respectively). The 
earliest paper that I actually have in possession on IP side 
is łProcessing of Tiros Cloud Cover Pictures on a Digital 
Computer˛ by Albert Arking, 1967, but I'm sure the literature 
is much older. It's easy for the geometry based guys to leave 
all this stuff out and vice versa.˛ Alvy Ray Smith

The very first computer graphics company was formed by two of 
the leading researchers of the day, Drs. David C. Evans and 
Ivan E. Sutherland. Aptly named Evans & Sutherland, it 
provided a vector system comprised of custom designed 
hardware and software previously available only to one of a 
kind, multi million dollar military sites.
Dicomed is founded as a manufacturer of hardware and 
software products to apply computer graphic technology to the 
field of medical radiology. Their systems operate by scanning 
x-ray films, converting the information into digital data, 
enhancing it and redisplaying the processed image. (See their 
web site at www.dicomed.com ). Still in business 30 years 
later, providing professional high resolution digital image 
capturing technologies.

1970's
Widespread commercial use of this early technology did 
not begin until the 1970ąs when early pioneers saw the 
potential in the broadcast video market for the new creative 
tools. Companies like Image West(LA), Dolphin Productions 
(New York) and Computer Image Corp (Denver, President Lee 
Harrison) used these realtime computer assisted video 
graphics machines to introduce new imagery to both broadcast 
clients and the viewers at home.
[BIO SNIP] Lee Harrison, the inventor of analog video-
based computer animation, was the founder of Computer Image 
Corporation(1969) in Denver, CO.; where the ANIMAC, 
Scanimate, C.A.E.S.A.R., and System IV analog animation 
devices were developed. Lee won an Emmy for SCANIMATE in 
1972.
	Relatively affordable commercial random access frame 
buffers became available in the mid to late 70ąs which opened 
up the market for CG production. The input for these earliest 
machines were often banks of patch wires, paper tape or punch 
cards, very different from today's mouse and graphic 
interfaces.
	These first million dollar commercial machines were 
mostly capable of only limited, video resolution raster based 
graphics. While their output was limited in most cases to 
videotaping or filming monitor screens, their imagery did 
introduce the public at large to the new art form. By the end 
of the decade affordable raster technology out paced the 
earlier vector graphic mainstay. 
€Pioneering work done by Jim Blinn at the Jet 
Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Pasadena California 
(started in 1975 by Bob Holzman). David Em (who would work 
with Alvy Ray Smith at Xerox PARC on Dick Shoup's Superpaint 
system in about 1974 or so) also later joined Jim at JPL to 
create some of the early serious computer art in raster form.
 €Nelson Max at Lawrence Livermore National 
Laboratories  uses CG to illustrate basic biologic research; 
the first łscientific visualizations˛.

1971
Gary Demos visits NASA AMES and Evans & Sutherland while 
researching a documentary film about computers for łDimension 
Films˛ in LA. It is there that he first meets Ivan Sutherland 
and expresses his ambitious desire to create complex and 
realistic high resolution CG images for films. (Gary is only 
about 21 years old at the time) Since most of the hardware 
and software technology that would make this possible does 
not yet exists, Gary joins E&S in hopes of creating these 
missing pieces. John Warnock ran the San Jose E&S office 
before going to NYIT, and Ivan himself was working on his own 
hidden surface solutions at the time. Gary helped develop a 
high precision łdata table˛ (table not tablet because it was 
4 feet by 5 feet) accurate to 100th of an inch for digitizing 
images. The table used two pens to define two simultaneous 
points in 3D space. Programming was done in assembly code on 
a PDP-11 with a Picture System 1 for vector display.
	Both Henry Gouroug and Bui Toi Phong worked on shading 
at E&S, so that area was well covered needless to say. Gary 
and the E&S team next tackled the challenge of building the 
first ever random access frame buffer. They began with the 
first 8 DRAM chips every produced, which came from a company 
in Texas called Mostek(sp?).

Star Wars (Twentieth Century Fox) 
The Death Star simulation was designed and created by 
pioneering algorithmic artist Larry Cuba. George Lucas was 
impressed both by Cubaąs early abstract CG film First 
Fig(1974) and the fact that he had worked with another 
pioneer of motion control and computer graphics John Whitney 
Sr. Ben Burt, the films sound designer, had been tasked to 
get the word out around town and track down bids for the 
work.
Cuba designed storyboards from the description of the 
scene in the script, and worked on the job at the University 
of Illinois Chicago. A 2D drawing program that Cuba designed 
with the GRASS language was modified to allow input of a 
third Z axis for every point entered on the digitizing 
tablet, creating the 3D representation of the Death Star 
surface. 
Using the Vector General based GRASS graphics system 
designed by Tom DeFanti, Larry worked night and day for 12 
weeks to produce 2 minutes of film of which 40 seconds 
appeared in the final film sequence. 
	[RENDER TIME QUOTE] ł(While the GRASS system was capable 
of real time animation) the real time capability came from 
the Vector General's hardware implementation of basic 
transformations, like translation, rotation and scaling.  
also the projection transformation that turns a 3D object 
into a 2D drawing, but it was only capable of a parallel 
projection (that is, no 'true perspective'). Since I needed 
perspective for this project, I was back to using software 
for the projection and therefore *not* able to animate the 
scene in real time. I was getting a frame rate of about two 
minutes of computation per frame and so the whole shot 
took about 12 hours.˛ Larry Cuba
(A rented Mitchell camera filmed the imagery off of the 
computer monitor) The finished footage was originally 
intended to be shot as a rear projected element live on stage 
with the actors in London, but greatly reduced production 
deadlines made that impossible. The full story as told by 
Larry Cuba himself:
[QUOTE] łAround two months from my deadline, I was sent 
a production schedule and I noticed that the live action 
shooting of the shot that my work was to be used in, was 
scheduled a month earlier than the delivery date specified on 
my contract.  So instead of having two months left to finish 
the shot, I had only one.
When I mentioned this to the Assistant Producer, he 
informed me that it was even worse than that because they 
required the film to be delivered 4 weeks earlier than 
shooting in order to have time to make back up copies (should 
anything happen to the footage during the live action 
filming).  So apparently, since I couldn't send out the shot 
immediately, we were already dead in the water.
The 'solution' he came back to me with was that they 
would rearrange the schedule and place that scene (the 
briefing room scene) on the last day that they had the large 
sound stage (they were shooting in England.  All 
communication went from me, in Chicago, to the Assistant 
Producer in LA, to the Producer, Gary Kurtz in London and 
then to Lucas and then the reverse trip back).  This would 
give me four more weeks to produce the shot (rather than the 
eight that I thought I had).
So with my schedule cut in half, I stepped up 
production.  I was getting three hours of sleep a night by 
sleeping on the sofa in the (over air conditioned) lab with 
the computers. computers generate a lot of heat so computer 
rooms need to be kept cool or  the computers will fail to 
work.
Working in this way, I was able to finish building the 
computer model of the Death Star and program the fly through 
sequence just in time for it to be filmed and sent off. But 
once I started the film run (which had to run continuously 
for 12 hours), the computer would crash about 30 minutes into 
it.  Up until this point, the occasional crash was not a 
problem.  reboot and keep going.  But now this was a 
disaster. I couldn't put the shot together filming in 30 
minute bursts.  (I could if I rewrote the program, but there 
was no time for that now).  We tried everything we could 
think of to get the system to stop crashing. (we even took 
the hard disk apart and cleaned it), but 30 minutes after 
every start, the system crashed.
It was getting late on Saturday night and I had to put 
the exposed film in the mail on Monday.  By 3am (my bedtime), 
I decided that it was useless.  On Monday morning, instead of 
sending out the film, I would have to call LA and tell them 
that I had failed to deliver and that our only recourse at 
this point was to shoot the scene blue screen and optically 
print my animation in later.
Since there was no more hope, I figured I would at least 
be more comfortable, so before I went to sleep, I turned off 
the air conditioning so I wouldn't freeze, and I started the 
shot from the beginning one more time (what the heck?).  This 
time it ran continuously throughout the night and Sunday 
morning, completing the shot just in time.˛ Larry Cuba
There was traditional hand animation done for the final 
four seconds of the bomb entering the death star exhaust port 
and exploding; completed by John Wash at Image West. 
Other computer graphic and video display images were 
created for Star Wars by several different people. John Wash, 
Jay Teitzell and Dan OąBannon at Image West created many 
electronic video graphic effects for the targeting computers 
and background tactical displays. Larry Cuba also completed 
several graphics seen in the DeathStar guard room when R2 and 
C3PO first tap into the central computer.
[SIGGRAPH FACTOID] The 1977 SIGGRAPH convention 
Electronic Film Show also ended with Larry Cubaąs work, 
although not as planned. Halfway through his film łFirst 
Fig˛ all the power went out in the hotel bringing it, and the 
show to a premature ending.

Jim Blinn produces the first in his series of animations for 
the The Mechanical Universe while at JPL. 
Jim Blinn also publishes his technique of bump mapping, 
completed as part of his graduate thesis at the University of 
Utah the previous year. His demonstration of the new shading 
code is shown as 128x128 resolution, 16 frame loop of a bumpy 
sphere. His initial method of calculating both the angle and 
amount of perturbation is later refined and simplified as an 
altitude description, allowing for incremental gray scale 
values to define intermediate angles of surface normals.

1980's
	The first digital computers used in CG were those in 
the Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) line including the 
early PDP-1, PDP10 and PDP-11 of the last decade. However 
because of their cost and high maintenance, these were 
restricted to large budget University and major production 
settings. Typical of this work is Jim Blinn at JPL creating 
the Voyager Flyby films, the Cosmos Series for Carl Sagan, 
and the Mechanical Universe project; all from about 1979 to 
1983.
The łworkstations˛ as we know it today were introduced 
in the early 1980s by companies such as Apple Computer and 
Silicon Graphics Inc. 
The consumer market for personal computer graphics began 
with the Macintosh personal computer and its MacDraw and 
MacPaint software in 1984. The Xerox Alto did of course pre-
date the Mac by a decade, but did not reach personal use in 
any numbers; itąs initial market was government and 
University settings.
Commercial CG production was boosted by the new 
generation of digital machines such as the (MORE INFO!) and 
the early Silicon Graphics workstations such as the IRIS 3130 
in 1989. At the same time, third party companies began 
providing specialized software to run on these new graphic 
platforms. For 2D graphic design and image processing, 
Photoshop was introduced for the Mac in 198?. Early 3D 
animation software for the higher end market included 
Wavefront(1987), Intelligent Light(198?), and Alias 
v1.0(1984). 
	The mid 1980ąs to early 1990ąs were a time of tremendous 
advances in technology and stunning creative breakthroughs. 
Companies such as Robert Abel and Associates, Triple-I, 
Magi/Synthavision, Omnibus, and Digital Productions created 
such memorable images as Sexy Robot (ABEL), Chromosaurs 
(PDI), and the Benson & Hedges(Digital Productions) 
commercials. 
The U.S. National Science Foundation began to provide 
supercomputer access to university research programs, 
including the University of Illinois Supercomputing Center.

Tron (Disney)
The first extensive use of 3D CGI animation for a 
feature film. This milestone project was originally boarded 
by Bill Kroyer and Jerry Rees and pitched to Disney by Steve 
Listberger. Bill and Jerry came up with the titles łComputer 
Image Choreographers˛ for their roles which were much more 
than traditional Animation Directors. The model motion and 
choreography, along with camera blocking and motion paths 
were all sketched out in exacting detail to be passed on and 
realized precisely by four CG production houses.
[TRON FACTOID] The largest format pencil tests ever! The 
Disney art and animation team that were previsualizing the CG 
for the film, never had any way to view a traditional pencil 
test. The first time they got a chance to see their planned 
motion scenes was only after the CG was created, rendered and 
output to 70mm film. Because of a technical limitations at 
Disney, the film was actually rear projected in the screening 
room.
So who did what CG on TRON? Robert Abel & Associates 
created the title sequence for the film, and the entry to the 
digital computer world. Digital Effects created the little 
bit character. Mathematical Applications Group Inc. 
(MAGI) created the light cycles and most of the recognizers. 
Information International Inc. (Triple-I) created 
Sarkąs carrier, the solar sailer, and the MCP character 
sequences near he end of the film. 
In total, there was actually only about 15 minutes of 
computer generated imagery created for the film, supervised 
by Richard Taylor. The majority of effects were accomplished 
by traditional animation techniques involving tens of 
thousands of hand rotoscoped individual frames of artwork. 
1982/83 
Where the Wild Things Are (Test done at MAGI): The first 
instance of digital compositing for motion picture work. The 
character animation was done at Disney (lead by Glen Keane,) 
and the cg backgrounds, rendering, painting, and compositing 
was done at Magi/Synthavision.  Jon Lasseter was the 
official Disney-Magi liaison. Ken Perlin supervised the 
project, with the CG work lead by Chris Wedge and Jan Carlee 
(both now at Blue Sky.). Software was by Ken Perlin, 
Christine Chang, Gene Miller, and Josh Pines. Look for many 
more details in the Companies Chapter!

[Quantel looses PATENTS ISSUE] 
łBritish company Quantel has been asserting a set of 
patents against companies for about a decade now, patents 
that many of us in the digital imaging and computer graphics 
business believed were invalid.  These 1980s-vintage patents 
covered airbrushing (digital painting with soft-edged 
brushes), digital image compositing (!), pressure-sensitive 
stylus, mixing paints on a window called a palette, etc.  I 
and my colleagues have long believed these notions to be too 
simple to be worthy of "invention" hence patent coverage.  
Furthermore, if anyone were to deserve credit for the 
"invention", it certainly wasn't the Quantel people in the 
1980s but rather several of the many practitioners (in the US 
mainly) in the 1970s.
Jim Blinn, Lance Williams, and I tried to help save a 
British company called Spaceward from these patents in a 
London trial in 1989. We were unsuccessful, largely, I 
believe, because we didn't have any hard evidence - no code, 
no program. This changed in September 1997.  Quantel sued 
Adobe, well-known US producer of popular software products 
such as Photoshop, for patent infringement on US versions of 
the UK patents that had been held against Spaceward.   The 
trial was held in Wilmington, Delaware.  The following 
colleagues joined me in helping Adobe this time:  Marc Levoy, 
Christie Barton, David Em, Dick Phillips, Jim Blinn (by 
deposition), and others.
The Adobe attorneys did a great job of gathering 
evidence, including hard evidence this time.  They obtained 
actual code that I had written in 1977 and 1978 and 
recompiled it under Windows.  So I was able to demonstrate 
directly to the jury exactly what we had done in the 1970s - 
in this case I was showing the first full-color (RGB, or 24-
bit) digital paint program, which of course did many of the 
things Quantel claimed to have invented in the 1980s!  Marc 
Levoy's 1978 full-color paint program (the second one) was 
similarly found and recompiled and shown to the jury.
Long story short:  The jury found all five patents at 
issue invalid (and that Adobe was innocent of infringement).˛
-Alvy Ray Smith

Siri co-founder backs Helix for its voice ID tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
15:02:47 UTC
00:02:47 KST

For years, websites have relied on technology like CAPTCHA to prove that the user on the other end is human. More recently, social media platforms have turned to photos or videos to verify users’ identities. Now, a startup called Helix is betting that voice technology can do the same job, without requiring users to hand over sensitive personal information.
The voice technology, which can run directly on a user’s device, has attracted backing from Siri co-founder Dag Kittlaus, who will also act as an adviser.
The company raised $6.2 million in funding in a round led by Chicago Ventures, with participation from BAM Ventures, Aglaé Ventures, Corazon Capital, Press On Ventures, Tusk Ventures, Yonder Ventures, Rule 30, and Brown Angel Group.
The startup was founded by Alex Oberg, Anna Dorofiyenko, and Mike Hall in 2025. Oberg previously worked at Ticketmaster, which acquired his startup; Dorofiyenko led data science teams at Live Nation and Zillow; and Hall has worked at Nike and Tinder, where he helped develop the initial matching algorithm.
At Ticketmaster, Oberg played a role in creating Verified Fan, which is designed to keep bots out of the platform. As AI advanced, he started thinking along the same lines for a new solution.
“As AI started to come up in the last two years, I was realizing that it’s going to make it increasingly difficult to determine who’s human and who’s not on the internet. Identity on the internet’s always been about proxies for identity, right? It’s your email, it’s your phone, it’s your IP address, it’s your device fingerprint, it’s your device ID,” Oberg said.
He noted that with the rise of AI agents like Instinct and Muse, the industry needs to rethink human identity on the internet and rely on biometric signals like voice, which is where Helix comes in.
Its core technology can run directly on a device to determine whether someone is human and estimate their age. The company is also running pilots to explore whether voice can be used as a biomarker to detect conditions such as drunkenness or distress.
The company can deploy its technology to replace or supplement CAPTCHA and help block bot attacks. Helix said that because its model can run locally even on an iPhone 13, the cost of deploying the technology is minimal. The startup said one of its customers is Zeel, an in-home healthcare provider that uses Helix’s tech to verify the identities of providers visiting customers’ homes.
Oberg said verifying workers, such as cabdrivers, is another use case the startup is exploring. He also said that age-verification regulations for social media platforms around the world are forcing users to trade privacy for access. Helix’s voice technology, he said, could offer an alternative.
“There’s like an avalanche of regulation coming down because essentially society has decided children should not be able to use the internet as adults. That has created a bit of a strawman argument that everyone needs to trade their privacy for the sake of security and child safety. We are that company that’s saying, nope, don’t agree. It’s a four-second voice challenge,” he said.
The CEO also emphasized the limitations of Helix’s technology, noting that it cannot reliably detect whether someone is lying. He added that its voice technology doesn’t identify individual speakers — while verifying them being unique humans — and claimed that even if the company stores a voiceprint, it cannot be used to reconstruct a person’s voice.
AI-powered fraud is also a growing problem in phone calls. But Helix believes its technology isn’t yet capable of reliably detecting AI agents during live calls.
Siri co-founder Kittlaus said that voice-identification technology has finally reached a point where it works reliably, positioning Helix to scale as AI-powered fraud increases. He also said that Helix’s work to compress its models gives the startup a cost advantage.
“What folks at Helix are doing is, instead of teaching computers how to understand speech, these guys are understanding what the speech of the speaker actually means, what’s going on with them, if they are lying, are they impaired? That side of it is fascinating to me within the larger picture that I just described,” he told TechCrunch.

Iceberg's https:// clones, fetches, pulls and pushes, and Metacello's github:// loads, go to this CORS proxy: each request goes to the proxy's URL followed by the host and the path of the repository, such as github.com/pharo-project/pharo.git. The proxy sees the code and any credentials that pass through it, so choose only one that you run or trust: the user name and token that a push asks for go only through My proxy, or straight to the host with None, never through the site's default. With None, the requests go to the repository itself, which works only for a server that lets this page in (CORS). This browser keeps your choice; a link cannot set it.

Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
14:18:08 UTC
23:18:08 KST

Researchers at Google DeepMind have unveiled a new AI model designed to unravel how changes in our DNA affect different cells, giving scientists a more detailed view of a notoriously difficult problem that could hold important clues to the causes of disease — and point the way to new treatments.
Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
DeepMind’s new DNA model better predicts how mutations affect different cells, potentially opening paths to treatment.
AlphaGenome 2 is the successor to DeepMind’s genome-predicting AI model AlphaGenome, which was released last year. While nearly every cell in the human body carries the same DNA, different types of cells — from heart muscle cells and skin cells to immune cells fighting an infection — switch different genes on and off, and those patterns can change depending on what a cell is doing. As a result, the same genetic variant can have very different effects depending on the type and state of the cell.
The new model is designed to capture those differences, predicting the effects of genetic variants on individual cell types and states. Google said in a blog post published Wednesday that it offers a much finer-grained view than broader models like AlphaGenome, potentially revealing disease-relevant effects in specific cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.
AlphaGenome 2 was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues to give it that more detailed view. DeepMind says the model effectively turns static cell atlases — huge data repositories that map and catalog individual cells in detail — “into a predictive engine for human genetics.” According to the company, AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that can change gene expression in cells than its previous state-of-the-art model.
Notably, the researchers found that AlphaGenome 2 could also make predictions about new types of cells and biological states without needing to be retrained. It could also identify gaps in experimental data, potentially helping scientists decide what to investigate next in the lab.
For Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, the big breakthrough is “tying human genetics to cell biology.” AlphaGenome 2 gives researchers a way to drill down on genetic variants identified in large populations, to see what effects they may be having on a cellular level, and potentially connect those effects to disease, he told The Verge.
Google DeepMind’s genomics lead Žiga Avsec told The Verge that this specificity is important if you have a goal like figuring out how to treat a particular disease. “When you develop drugs, you’re targeting specific proteins and specific cell types,” he explained, which makes having this kind of granularity vital.
Building a model like AlphaGenome 2 has only recently become possible thanks to new technologies that can capture individual cells and their states at high resolution and create the vast datasets needed to train it, Avsec said. DeepMind is now working to improve its genetics models by generating more data, including for cell states that aren’t represented well today. Avsec said future versions could also potentially be trained on data “across multiple species,” giving the models a broader view of biology. Longer term, he said models like AlphaGenome 2 could feed into efforts to create “virtual cells,” digital simulations designed to mimic biological systems.
Although Avsec said he views AlphaGenome 2 as a successor to AlphaGenome, it isn’t replacing it any time soon. He said its more detailed predictions come at a computational cost and are “more expensive” to produce than those of its predecessor, he said. Those demands would have made it impractical to use AlphaGenome 2 to produce the genome-wide Atlas covering “every possible DNA letter change in the human genome” that DeepMind released in September.
Google says it is making AlphaGenome 2 available for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API from today, with a limited “private preview” for commercial research.
The model is the latest in a growing array of efforts by Google and rival AI labs to use the technology to tackle major problems in science and medicine. Pushmeet Kohli, who heads DeepMind’s AI for science research, has hinted that more impressive scientific results are on the way, and the organization is expected to open an automated materials science lab in the UK soon. Anthropic, meanwhile, has been experimenting with drug design and given Claude a wet lab, while OpenAI has been mowing down an impressive amount of longstanding problems in mathematics and related fields.

Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends. Google’s Tabletop AI experiment lets you build custom collaboration apps
Tabletop provides customizable, collaborative spaces for all your personal planning needs.

Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
14:10:46 UTC
23:10:46 KST

Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex
Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine
Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then runatuin resume
Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me.
These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on exe.dev, a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on.
It’s a familiar problem!
I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of .bash_history. But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds.
Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things.
Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily.
Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work.
Atuin Threads
That is why we built Atuin Threads.
Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop.
Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this.
Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, run your own, or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too.
Run atuin resume, and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post!
It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever.
Right now, we support
- Claude Code
- Codex
- Pi
- Omp
- OpenCode
with more agents coming soon.
MCP
With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context.
Our MCP is available as atuin mcp, and can be automatically installed with
atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode
There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples:
Work that never shipped
I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better.
These sessions contain the code that never made it into main, as well as my initial prompts and iteration. Subsequent agents can use this to figure out exactly what I want, without me having to write up a giant spec.
Object store outage
With all the security issues going on in the industry recently, we rolled our keys as a precaution. One of the new object store keys did not have the correct permissions for avatar uploads! We didn’t notice straight away 😬
My daily Sentry triage agent picked up on it, and traced the failure down to a command run earlier that day. I hadn’t gotten around to reading it yet, but prompting another agent with
seeing some tigris avatar issues?
led to the agent discovering the previous investigation, highlighting the cause, and developing the fix much faster than if it had done the whole thing from scratch.
Forking threads across machines
Before releasing Threads, I did some testing on a variety of machines and setups.
One machine did not perform well. The agent investigating proposed that this was because of poor IO performance, but that it needed something with a faster disk to confirm.
I forked the session onto my MacBook, and it continued from exactly where it left off. With the faster SSD, the investigation concluded that slow disk was only part of the story - we could speed up imports elsewhere, too.
Once the benchmarks were complete, the thread running on the original machine could pull the results from the Mac and build a fix. I didn’t have to copy-paste anything or co-ordinate across machines, and the data is now part of the record of my work.
Teams
While this is tremendously useful as a solo engineer, it gets even more interesting with a team.
So much of what we do never makes it into Git, issue trackers, or documentation. The context behind that work ends up scattered across individual agent sessions. What if the rest of the team could learn from it too? What if we could hand off an agent thread just like a Git branch?
We’re building opt-in session sharing for teams, and would love to hear from folks using agents day to day. If this sounds useful to you, please get in touch!
While agents have radically changed my daily workflow, shell history isn’t going anywhere, and is arguably more useful than ever. Threads is an extension of the same idea that started Atuin in the first place - the history of your work should be useful, accessible, and yours to keep.
Threads is out in Atuin 18.24+
- Install or update Atuin with curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | sh
- Run atuin resume to get started
- Use the MCP with atuin mcp install
Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions or feedback!

Apple is killing its Support Community forum next week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
14:02:11 UTC
23:02:11 KST

It’s the end of the road for the Apple Support Community. The dedicated discussion forum, which gave Apple users a place to exchange advice, troubleshoot, and generally chat about Apple products, has been placed into read-only mode, with a message from the company announcing that the Support Community will shut down for good on November 20th.
Apple is killing its Support Community forum next week
The Apple Support Community platform is now read-only, and will permanently close on November 20th.
Here’s the full banner notice that’s currently displayed on the website:
“The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site. We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.”
The Apple Support Community has undergone several name changes over the years, but its history as an online forum for providing user-to-user tech support goes back to 1998, when it first launched as the Apple Tech Exchange. Apple hasn’t specified what will happen to the decades worth of Support Community posts when the platform shuts down next week. Presumably, they’ll all disappear with it.
In a statement to MacRumors, Apple said it decided to sunset the Apple Support Community after a careful evaluation of strategy and customer needs. We have reached out to Apple for comment.

Plurai wants to help AI agents work better using the same approach that helped get self-driving cars to roads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

AI agents are all the rage, but they’re not quite as capable as their purveyors would have you believe.
Efforts to benchmark agents doing complex tasks show that they aren’t typically reliable enough to function without close supervision. LiveBench 2.0 shows Claude Fable 5.2 and ChatGPT-6 Astra succeeding on 82.9 and 75.6 out of 100 tasks, respectively, and an effort by the AI infrastructure company EON to test agents in a simulated corporate environment found the most successful model tested, Claude Opus 4.8, performed tasks at 76.8% accuracy.
Now, a startup known as Plurai wants to boost those numbers with the same techniques that put self-driving cars on the street: Simulations using synthetic data based on a company’s own digital systems, meant to prepare models to tackle difficult edge cases.
Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked for Nexar, which develops autonomous driving technology. Kadar worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software.
“The moment that we saw the wave of AI agents, we saw the same pattern: That it is very easy to build a demo, but [hard] to get something that will be reliable and cost effective,” Kadar told TechCrunch. “Since we saw the same pattern, the same pitch was that we want to build this simulation layer.”
On Wednesday, the startup said it had raised $13 million in seed funding to make that happen. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity, and Mercer.
Like the end-to-end models trained to drive cars, AI agents are probabilistic systems operating in unpredictable environments. When pressed by customers, agents tasked with booking travel can ignore spending policies. Or, when tasked with querying one database, agents can reliably provide an answer, but combining information from multiple datasets tends to gum up the works. A long conversation with a customer service bot can overwhelm an agent with too much context and lead to wrong turns.
To fix that, Plurai creates a digital twin of the company’s electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools that an agent will have access to in production. It then maps all the possible flows of the agents and uses that graph to prepare the model with evaluations and fixes for possible edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools like Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Cursor.
However, Kadar says the company’s real promise is using the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customer needs. Tests performed in cooperation with Nvidia and Nebius showed the company’s models outperforming midtier frontier models at lower costs.
“We can take a large language model, we can take the task, decompose it into a smaller task using the simulation, train [an open-weight] model, and using the simulation, verify that the quality is higher or comparable to the frontier model, and an order or two orders of magnitude cost reduction,” he said.
Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed Plurai as an angel investor, said the company’s edge comes from understanding failure modes in production, and generating synthetic data to tune models. As businesses try to optimize their AI expense, Plurai’s approach could prove a real advantage, since IT leaders are seeing that “frontier-capable models are out of distribution with my specific data, and the cost of these things isn’t sustainable in the long term,” Miyara said.
Plurai hopes analogies between AI agents in physical and digital environments can prove predictive: While powerful general AI models are imbuing robots with fascinating capabilities, they aren’t yet reliable enough to be deployed widely. Meanwhile, robots powered by AI models built for specific tasks are in the field right now, working for customers and gathering valuable real-world data.
“My view is that no matter how smart OpenAI and Anthropic model will be — and they will be much smarter — they will not know your business and your policy,” Kadar said.

Thanksgiving Kale Slaw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11

Thanksgiving Kale Slaw
Make a holiday-worthy slaw with shredded kale, cabbage, crispy fried shallots, and a shallot oil-infused maple Dijon vinaigrette.
Serves4 to 8
Makesabout 6 cups
Prep20 minutes
Cook15 minutes
Why You’ll Love Thanksgiving Kale Slaw
- This salad is one of my favorite things on the holiday table. It’s the perfect balance to all that heavy holiday food, and delicious enough to eat all season long.
- It’s make-ahead- and leftovers-friendly. All of the ingredients can be prepped (and even assembled) ahead of time so you can cross one time-sensitive dish off your list. Plus, the leftovers don’t get soggy!
- The shallots do triple duty. This little workhorse ingredient gives you a punchy raw bite, crispy fried shallots on top, and a deeply flavorful infused oil for the vinaigrette.
Nearly 10 years ago, I engineered a feat of unimaginable success: I made a genuinely crowd-pleasing Thanksgiving salad that can be made ahead of time (so I can stay out of my mom’s way) and actually keeps well as leftovers, provided there are any to box up at all. Today it’s still one of my favorite salads and things on the holiday table — the crunchy texture and bright flavor perfectly balance the richer dishes. That said, I developed it for a different time in my life and an entirely different circumstance.
When I made that salad, I was living in Houston and driving it over to my parents’ house as my contribution to dinner. Now I’m in Brooklyn and, more often than not, I’m the one hosting and making the whole freaking dinner in my little apartment kitchen. Suddenly, a little extra effort feels like a lot. So I thought maybe I could distill down the most important flavors of that salad and make something that still felt special, but perhaps a bit less fussy.
I kept the lacinato kale, but swapped shredded Brussels sprouts (a real time suck) for cabbage. Some chopped dates and roasted nuts give texture and little flavorful bits. The one non-negotiable: fried shallots. Frying shallots might be a little annoying, but it’s simple, can be done a day ahead, and truly makes the salad a star. In fact, I’m using shallots three ways: raw in the salad for some punch and crunch, fried to a shattering crisp, and then the infused oil is the base for a maple Dijon vinaigrette. The salad has everything I need to feel holiday-worthy without adding too much to my plate (pun intended).
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“This is a unique and delicious slaw! Don’t skip the fried shallots. They add a wonderful crunch to the slaw. Plus using the shallot oil in the dressing adds a great depth of flavor to the kale/cabbage combo. I can’t wait to serve this up at the table this year.” —Kristina, November 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
I’m a professional recipe developer, but when I’m asked, people are often surprised to hear that my favorite food to eat, develop, and style for photos is salad — which is why I created my column, Salad Person. Whether I’m on my weekly (or more) farmers market crawl or meticulously surveying the grocery store produce, I’m constantly geeking out over seasonal fruits and vegetables. I love making salads that look gorgeous, taste even better, and will have your friends texting you for the recipe!
Key Ingredients in Thanksgiving Kale Slaw
- Kale: A base of lacinato (or Tuscan) kale will hold up to the dressing for days without losing the crunch factor.
- Cabbage: A little green cabbage breaks up all the kale, and retains its crunch even when dressed.
- Dates: Sweet, chewy dates add little pops of sweetness and textural variety.
- Shallots: Punchy raw shallots add a boost of sharp allium flavor, while crispy fried shallots make the perfect crunchy topping. Use the infused oil to boost the vinaigrette’s flavor.
Helpful Swaps
- Instead of olive oil, I love the buttery flavor of algae cooking oil.
- Swap out pecans or walnuts for roasted pistachios or almonds. Or, for a nut-free salad, try toasted pumpkin or sunflower seeds.
- Use dried cherries or Craisins instead of dates.
Salad Person is my column dedicated to making better, more delicious salads at home that you’re actually excited to eat. Each month, I’ll provide tips and techniques so you can enjoy them as much as I do — which is a lot!
Thanksgiving Kale Slaw Recipe
Make a holiday-worthy slaw with shredded kale, cabbage, crispy fried shallots, and a shallot oil-infused maple Dijon vinaigrette.
Prep time 20 minutes
Cook time 15 minutes
Makes about 6 cups
Serves 4 to 8
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
For the fried shallots and dressing:
- 1 cup olive oil
- 4 medium shallots, thinly sliced (1 1/2 cups)
- 3/4 teaspoon kosher salt, divided, plus more as needed
- 1/4 cup Champagne or white wine vinegar
- 1 clove garlic, finely grated or minced
- 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard
- 1 tablespoon maple syrup
- 1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, plus more as needed
For the slaw base:
- 1 medium bunch flat-leaf or lacinato kale (10 ounces total), stems removed and leaves thinly sliced crosswise into strips (3 1/2 to 4 packed cups)
- 2 cups finely shredded green cabbage (1/4 medium cabbage)
- 1 medium shallot, thinly sliced (1/2 cup)
- 1/3 cup fresh parsley or mint leaves, or a combination
- 1/2 cup roasted pecans or walnuts, coarsely chopped, divided
- 1/2 cup dried Medjool dates (5 to 6), pitted and coarsely chopped, divided
Instructions
Make the fried shallots and dressing:
- Line a plate with paper towels. Place 1 cup olive oil and 4 thinly sliced medium shallots in a medium skillet. Cook over medium heat, stirring frequently, until the shallots are golden-brown and crisp, about 15 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer the shallots to the plate and season with 1/4 teaspoon of the kosher salt.
- Transfer 1/3 cup of the shallot oil to a jar with a lid; reserve the remaining oil for another use. Add 1/4 cup Champagne vinegar, 1 finely grated garlic clove, 1 tablespoon Dijon mustard, 1 tablespoon maple syrup, the remaining 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt, and 1/4 teaspoon black pepper to the jar. Seal the jar and shake until combined. Taste and season with more kosher salt and black pepper as needed. (Alternatively, whisk the dressing together in a medium bowl.)
Assemble the slaw:
- Place 1 bunch thinly sliced flat-leaf kale leaves, 2 cups finely shredded green cabbage, 1 thinly sliced medium shallot, 1/2 cup fresh herb leaves, 1/4 cup of the coarsely chopped roasted pecans, 1/4 cup of the coarsely chopped dates, and half of the fried shallots in a large bowl. Add the dressing and toss to combine.
- Sprinkle with the remaining 1/4 cup coarsely chopped roasted pecans, 1/4 cup coarsely chopped dates, and fried shallots.
Recipe Notes
Make ahead
- You can fry the shallots up to 1 day ahead and store in an airtight container at room temperature. Refrigerate the oil.
- Prepare the dressing, kale, and cabbage up to 1 day ahead. Refrigerate the dressing and greens in separate airtight containers.
- The dressed slaw (without shallots) can sit at room temperature for up to 2 hours without wilting, making it a great make-ahead or buffet dish. Wait until just before serving to toss and top with the fried shallots so they stay crunchy.
Storage
- Leftover shallot oil can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 1 month.
- Leftover slaw can be refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 3 days.

I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
13:56:05 UTC
22:56:05 KST

Every TV company is spying on you, not just LG. Like other tech companies, they collect lots of information, and while some is necessary for products to work, not all of it is — and could include details you’d prefer to keep private. Many customers are concerned about how TVs and streaming devices might be spying: listening to what you say, taking screenshots of everything you watch, storing sensitive information on your TV, and sharing your data with the cloud.
I asked every TV manufacturer 17 questions about how they spy on you
After LG was accused of spying through its TVs, I wanted to see how other TV companies were collecting and protecting our data.
To find out what TV and streaming device companies are doing, I decided to ask every one to explain itself. I put together 17 yes-or-no questions, like “Do your TVs store any recorded audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?” so that companies couldn’t just link to a confusing and legalese-ridden privacy policy. TV users deserve to know the answers.
Company representatives providing responses
Amazon: Eric Sveum, PR manager
Apple: Emily Ewing, public relations manager
Google: Alex García-Kummert, spokesperson
LG Electronics: Chris De Maria, director of public relations
Roku: Sarah Novatt, spokesperson
Samsung: Frank Giancamilli, corporate communications senior manager
TCL: Rob Manfredo, head of communications and events
One month ago, I invited 11 companies, including Amazon, Apple, Google, Hisense, LG, Panasonic, Roku, Samsung, Sony, TCL, and Walmart’s Vizio to share those answers. We now have answers from the top three TV manufacturers as well as every major streaming device company. Some companies declined to answer. Below, you can see and compare how each company answered (or failed to answer) each question and then decide how you feel. (One company, Hisense, ignored our emails entirely.)
As you’ll see them say, some of this data collection is opt-in, and you can often opt out. We know that many TVs use automatic content recognition (ACR) to figure out potentially everything we’re watching, and use that information to tailor ads, gather audience metrics, and serve up content recommendations based on our viewing habits. But though it sometimes seems like it’s required during the cavalcade of agreements thrown at us during setup, you can generally stop ACR even after you’ve agreed to it.
Opting out might not be as effective as it should be, however. A recent Northeastern University study found that Walmart’s Vizio kept on sending data after an opt-out (Vizio told me it was “routine operational data used to support the Vizio experience,” not ACR), while traffic with both Samsung and Roku was limited, but not stopped completely.
Below are the answers to our 17 questions. You will notice that some companies would not answer yes or no. We’ve also noted where companies declined to answer at all or ignored the questions. If any company becomes willing to directly answer our questions, we’ll add their responses.
1. Do your TVs ever use their embedded microphones, or the microphones in their remotes, to listen to sound in a customer’s home?
Amazon:
No. Fire TV includes voice functionality to help customers use their devices and get to content they love and fast, not to surveil homes. The microphones on our voice remotes are designed to only work when the mic button on the remote is physically pressed. And TVs with hands-free Alexa are designed to detect the wake word (and only the wake word) before connecting to Alexa. No audio is stored or sent to the cloud unless the device detects the wake word. Customers can also turn off the microphones at any time. Every Fire TV smart television that has microphones also has a physical button or switch that disables the microphone.
Apple:
Apple TV 4K will use its far-field microphones and the Always On Processor strictly to listen for the Siri wake word. The Always On Processor does not process or act on any other sounds in the home. Users have full control over this and can turn off “Siri” or “Hey Siri” as a wake word, or disable Siri entirely. When using the Siri Remote, users must actively press and hold the microphone button for it to start listening.
Google:
If Google Assistant or Gemini is enabled or available, microphones (built-in hands-free ‘Hey Google’ or remote push-to-talk button) listen for activation triggers. Microphones remain in passive standby until triggered by hotword or button press.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
Voice recognition is off by default and operates only if the user has opted in by accepting the Voice Information Agreement. Even if the user has opted in, they need to take additional steps for the microphone to be used. They must either press the microphone button on the remote control or they can use Hands-free Voice Control on supported models.
Hands-free Voice Control is disabled unless a user opts into this feature and then uses a wake-word. Wake-word detection is performed locally on the TV. If no wake word is detected, the audio is processed locally, promptly deleted, and is not stored, converted to text, or transmitted.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
While Roku TVs don’t have built-in microphones, some Roku remotes do. Standard voice remotes listen only while the mic button is held, and hands-free remotes can be switched off.
Samsung:
No, for private monitoring. Samsung TVs do not listen to or record private conversations.
The TV’s embedded microphone only listens locally for the specific wake-up word (like “Hi, Bixby”) and ignores all other sounds, while the remote control microphone only activates when the customer physically presses the button.
Sony:
Sony did not provide an answer to this question.
TCL:
Some TCL TVs and remotes have microphones. Users can activate those microphones to use voice assistance features provided through third-party operating systems or applications. Those third parties control whether the voice features are available and how they are used, under their own terms and privacy policies.
Vizio:
Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.

3. Do your TVs transmit any audio, or transcripts based on audio, captured in the home?
Amazon:
When customers speak to Alexa by pressing the mic button on the remote or using their chosen wake word, a recording of the request is sent to Amazon’s cloud, where a text transcript of the request is created to help Alexa provide a response. No audio is captured without the customer invoking Alexa—either by pressing the mic button or saying the wake word—and customers can easily review exactly what they asked and what Alexa heard, delete their recording, or even choose not to save them at all.
Apple:
Siri AI processes user requests using on-device processing, and when a request needs more powerful AI models, it extends those same on-device privacy protections to the cloud through a groundbreaking infrastructure called Private Cloud Compute (PCC). When Private Cloud Compute is handling users’ requests, their personal data is not stored nor made accessible to Apple, or anyone else, and outside experts can verify this privacy promise at any time.
For moments when users ask a question that requires up‑to‑date information, Siri AI can go out to the web and find it, then use Private Cloud Compute to generate an answer. Searches and requests are associated with a random identifier — a long string of letters and numbers — not a user’s Apple Account.
Google:
If Voice & Audio Activity is turned on, when voice features are activated (via hotword or remote button), captured audio or transcripts are transmitted to Google cloud servers for processing and fulfilling commands. If VAA is turned off, these are deleted.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
Yes, but only if voice recognition has been enabled (by opting in) and activated (by pushing the remote control microphone button or using the wake word). When voice recognition is activated, the TV displays an on-screen indication that voice recognition is active and listening for the user’s command. Once the user finishes the voice command, the command is transmitted to our server, where it is converted into text and processed to respond to the command.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
Roku TVs don’t have microphones. Voice-enabled remotes let people control their Roku devices by voice, as described in our privacy policy.
Samsung:
No, for ambient or background listening. Samsung TVs do not passively monitor, record, or transmit audio from your home. Audio is only captured and transmitted when you actively initiate a voice command (such as pressing the microphone button on your remote or using the wake word). This voice input is processed securely to fulfill your requests, improve services, and support connected features under our voice privacy policies.

5. Do your TVs store or transmit data on what content viewers watch or listen to through the TV?
Amazon:
Yes. For example, customers can opt in to allow Fire TV to collect certain viewing information like what shows they’ve watched in third-party apps to improve and personalize their experience, including by displaying shows and movies in a Continue Watching row on the Fire TV home screen. Customers can manage that setting anytime via their device’s Privacy Settings.
Apple:
Apple did not provide a direct answer to this question.
Google:
[Google TV] stores and transmits viewing history, watchlists, and app interactions for rentals/purchases on GTV and FreePlay. We do not have viewing history on third party apps.
Hisense:
Hisense did not respond to The Verge’s questions despite five attempts to make contact.
LG:
If the user has agreed to the Viewing Information Agreement, viewing information may be collected or processed in certain circumstances, including the following:
- ACR: Where ACR is available and enabled, ACR-related information may be collected and processed to identify content being viewed from supported sources. ACR uses audio fingerprinting technology to identify content rather than collecting screenshots, screen recordings, video recordings, voice recordings, or other audio recordings from the TV. To operate ACR services, LG may process content-identification fingerprints together with device information, content source information, network information, and consent settings needed to support the feature. ACR is optional and is turned off by default, and users can disable the feature at any time through the TV settings. ACR does not operate within third-party streaming apps.
- LG Channels: When a user streams content through LG Channels, information about the content being viewed is processed and sent to our servers so we can provide the requested streaming service.
- Voice Recognition: When users make voice commands, those commands and current viewing information (such as channel number and program name, and whether the source is an antenna or set-top-box) are sent to the server to process the voice commands and provide appropriate responses.
- Usage Information: Certain viewing information may also be collected as part of usage information relating to how the user interacts with the TV and its services, such as information about content selected for viewing or channels the user switches to.
Panasonic:
Panasonic did not provide an answer to this question.
Roku:
We collect streaming activity as described in our privacy policy. Smart TV Experience, which can identify other content on screen, is off by default in the US and is enabled only if the user opts in.
Samsung:
Yes, but only for TV programming and app viewing history. Samsung TVs do not monitor or transmit your personal files or private media.
Sony:
Sony did not provide an answer to this question.
TCL:
TCL collects limited data only for diagnostics and product improvement from some models of TCL Smart TVs. This collection is disclosed to users at setup and in TCL’s privacy notice, uses pseudonymization to prevent user profiling, and can be turned off by the user.
Vizio:
Vizio did not provide an answer to this question.
