Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
10:48:40 UTC
19:48:40 KST

Using voltage glitching to unleash the A100 in my mining card
On this page
Summary
I’ve discovered a voltage fault injection vulnerability on the GA100 die, allowing an operator to blow arbitrary fuses. Utilizing this vulnerability, I’ve converted my CMP 170HX 8GB card into what is effectively an A100-80G! Further, my unlocked cards actually perform ~1.2x faster than a retail A100 by having all functional SMs enabled (~120-126, die-lottery dependent), rather than the yield-safe 108 SMs NVIDIA chose for all production A100 cards. Finally, CMP-disabled features like NVLink, PCIe Gen4, NVJPG, NVDEC, MIG are all unlockable with this approach, though I haven’t specifically tested NVJPG/NVDEC/MIG.
Here’s how my “A100-80G” appears and functions.
NVIDIA uses fuses for product segmentation, security features, and other fun access control features - and crucially, there are several functions where blowing a fuse on an NVIDIA die can grant you more access, not less. In a properly secured design, a blown fuse should always induce a more restrictive state, because a blown fuse cannot be unblown in an economically feasible way. NVIDIA’s design allows one to relax restrictions by blowing more fuses!
In this post, I will go over the GA100 die, its fuse controller, the use of VFI, and future research directions. I’ve decided to publish some of the work that enabled my research here.
Acknowledgements
My work builds on prior research by Jon Pry and numerous others who have dedicated much of their time towards better understanding the GA100 die. I am disclosing my findings subsequent to another security researcher independently discovering the same vulnerability; I believe it to be in the best interest of the public to make this information publicly available. These findings were disclosed to NVIDIA’s product security team ahead of the publication of this article.
GA100 versions
The GA100 is an NVIDIA die that has been used to power almost 20 different SKUs - the A100 being the most well-known variant. I won’t delve into every SKU, but I will present the GA100 manifestations that matter to my work, covering the different versions of the CMP 170HX and the A100.
As fabbed, the GA100 die has 128 SMs, 12 FBPs, 5 NVDEC units, a PCIe Gen4 x16 controller, and depending on the framebuffer size, comes with 4-6 stacks of HBM co-packaged with the die. NVIDIA uses eFuses for yield-control and product segmentation–undifferentiated GA100s turn into more restrictive variants based on defect testing and manufacturer demand.
In one of the most extreme manifestations of product segmentation, the CMP 170HX, an Ethereum mining card with nominally 8 or 10 GB of application-exposed framebuffer capacity, actually comes with, respectively, ~80 and ~40 GB of HBM onboard! This work chiefly centers around how to fully unlock and use that capacity. Previous work has made great strides in unlocking the GA100 via software methods; VFI takes us across the last mile.
Hardware restrictions
So, how does NVIDIA utilize fuses to produce both a datacenter A100 and a mining CMP card from one die? To understand this, we need to take a closer look at the fuse controller located on the GA100.
The fuse controller is a block that contains 16,384 eFuses (512 rows of 32) and a bunch of logic surrounding that raw fuse macro. Its job is to perform fuse readout and programming, protect the underlying fuses, and provide usable “option words” to the rest of the die. These option words subsequently decide how the die functions and what features are enabled.
Each eFuse can be in one of two states (blown=1, unblown=0), and the 512 rows are divided into 4 regions:
- Regular fuses (rows 0-221). These are straightforward; often single (pairs of) fuses will map to an option word, such as OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM (an option word that determines whether further fuse programming is allowed or not). Regular fuses have built-in redundancy: for example, OPT_ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM consists of a PRI and RED (primary and redundant) fuse, in this case the primary instance is fuse 0 of row 0, and the redundant is fuse 0 of row 1. Some option words are scalars, such as OPT_X_COORDINATE, which is 9 bits wide and ostensibly holds the x-coordinate of the die on the fabbed wafer. Importantly, if a regular fuse is blown, there is basically no remedy to persistently unblow it (save for RIR later).
- Fuseless fuses (rows 222-487). This is a weird one. Apparently NVIDIA got frustrated with accidentally blowing regular fuses and ruining their engineering samples, and came up with a system to encode effective option words in a JTAG chain-like format (see this patent). Think about FF as essentially a script that describes what option words should have what values. FF fuses (excuse the RAS syndrome) concern most of the functionality we can unlock using VFI. This is because FF option words can be trivially cleared by simply writing new FF rows! We’ll about this more in depth, later. For now, you should know that NVIDIA also knows this, because under normal conditions, you are strictly prevented from performing any FF fuse blows.
- IFF fuses (rows 487-512). These contain instructions in a different format than the FF one. They’re out of scope for this post, and they’re mainly useful for on-the-fly reprogramming of fuse controller option words. They are usually not accessible in a production card.
- RIR fuses (8 rows of 32 fuses, which are technically not part of the 512 rows). These are provided by the designer of the fuse macro (TSMC datasheet here) and are essentially the first party designer’s intended “fuse repair” mechanism. The RIR section on a GA100 has space for 16 repair instructions, each overriding the value of an identified single fuse in the main 512 rows. Unfortunately for us, specifically in the 8 GB 170HX SKU, 15 of the 16 RIR words are all ones, and the 16th word encodes a useless repair instruction that can only be rarely leveraged for any interesting unlock. The story is different for the 10 GB SKU, but that’s a matter for another day…
There are two really interesting groups of fuses for the VFI-based unlock:
- “Control fuses”. The term comes from NVIDIA’s Tegra hardware headers, they use it to refer specifically to rows 0 and 1, which specify the values of highly security-sensitive option words.
- Fuseless fuses, which encode all of the interesting option words that decide whether a GA100 is born to be a measly mining card or an AI datacenter workhorse.
Before we name some of the FF-encoded option words, we’ll have to first understand the FF record format in a bit more detail, then talk about the die blocks that govern the features we are interested in.
Fuseless fuses
Each FF row is a 32-bit record. Bits 0–4 select a chain, bit 5 distinguishes FF from IFF (0 for FF), bits 6–15 select a 16-bit block, and bits 16–31 supply that block’s new value. The JTAG-chain picture from the patent is quite literal here: the controller builds the option data by replaying these records into chains. Fixed locations in each chain correspond to individual option words.
If two records address the same chain and block, the later record wins. For example, 0x0fe805c1 means chain 1, block 23, data 0x0fe8. Appending that record can clear an effective bit set by an earlier FF record. No physical fuse is unblown; a new row replaces the old 16-bit block. This works for FF-backed options, not the regular control fuses in rows 0 and 1.
Now that we know how FF words are encoded, here’s a list of the interesting words and their locations. These were discovered by a particularly helpful researcher who cross-compared FF values and effective option words from different GA100 SKUs in order to differentially understand the FF chain/block to option word mappings, as there is no known official mapping.
The acronyms FBIO/FBPA/FBP/TPC/GPC/PES/ROP all refer to microarchitectural elements, please see this diagram from the GA100 whitepaper to further understand how these are related to each other:
FBP is the internal NVIDIA term for a “framebuffer partition”, with 2 FBPs to one HBM stack. FBPAs are subpartitions, 2 FBPAs to one FBP. PES/ROP are blocks (seemingly graphics-related) that are required for an SM to function.
With this knowledge in hand, what if we could write new FF rows that set the _DISABLE words to be all zeroes, or at least, as permissive as possible given die defects? If we look at how the _DISABLE options are used in conjunction with other elements, we’ll quickly see that these _DISABLE words are the primary lever we have in preventing parts of the die from being “floorswept”. After illuminating the “what-if”, I’ll talk about the “how”: the exact application of voltage fault injection and the fuse controller safeguards we can defeat with VFI.
Floorsweeping
NVIDIA puts these options in charge of setting floorsweep signals, which will render a die element unreachable (and likely powered down). From experiments, I believe the floorsweep lines are specified in RTL, emanating from the fuse controller and terminating in individual functional blocks and controlling some master power/clock domain switch within the block. I have observed the floorsweeping behavior to correspond with very little latency with the value of the fuse controller’s effective status words for each functional block.
Let’s take FBP floorsweeping, for example. On one of my 8 GB cards, OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852: FBPs 1, 4, 6, and 11 were masked. The separate OPT_FBP_DEFECTIVE mask was 0x840, covering 6 and 11. After I reduced the FF-backed disable mask to 0x840 with a replacement FF row, the extra masks on 1 and 4 were gone, but the defective 6 and 11 stayed disabled. That leaves 10 of the die’s 12 FBPs in the effective mask. Functionally, FBPs 1 and 4, which refused register reads and writes when OPT_FBP_DISABLE was 0x852, became responsive after this fuse write.
Although the functional blocks can be “unfloorswept” with FF writes, this does not fully suffice to render the block fully available to an end application - the default framebuffer geometry configuration uses only a portion of each available HBM stack, for example.
To bypass that, we can utilize what is essentially a small modification to cmpunlocker’s method. The usual driver patch for the 8 -> 64 GB unlocks writes to a particular set of feature configuration words (FBPA_CFG, SM_SPEED_SELECT, etc.). The default values are chosen to succeed for the commonly found variant of the 170HX, which has the _DISABLE FF-derived option words preventing certain functional blocks from being used (any attempt to use them will return floorswept errors). With the unlocking FF burns in place, we can write even more permissive words into the configuration registers, resulting in what is functionally an A100-80G.
Achieving the FF burn
With the information we have, it seems straightforward that if one could blow arbitrary FF fuses, any GA100 could be fully unlocked to its maximum capability, as determined by die yield and the populated memory stacks. But how do we blow FF fuses? Let’s take a look at the fuse programming functionality of the fuse controller to understand more.
To request a fuse blow, one must write to the FUSEADDR, FUSEWDATA, and FUSECTRL registers belonging to the fuse controller. Although not nominally accessible to the host or to unprivileged requesters, with the Canary in the Crypto Mine ROP, opening up the responsible privilege level masks is trivial. And so, many researchers have attempted to coerce the fuse controller to blow fuses in the FF region. Some of our shared observations follow:
- The fuse controller has an internal FSM, and it indicates its current state via the FUSECTRL_STATE bits.
- The fuse controller enters a WRITE_PROGRAM state per each “hot” bit in the requested FUSEWDATA value. This tracks with the expected fuse programming behavior.
- However, unless a specific option word is cleared, writes to fuse addresses outside of the FPF range (rows 96-221) do not actually take place. Fuses in this region (believed to be “field programmable fuses” indicating a watermark of which ucode versions have run, alongside other field-relevant information) do take effect, and the fuse controller state machine behaves identically between FPF and non-FPF regions.
The specific option word I am referring to is OPT_SECURED_BURN_FEATURE_ENABLE (“SBFE”), and it is set to be 1 in all production cards. When this option word is clear, fuse programming is allowed in any address. When it is set, only FPF fuses may be blown. To date, no one has found any way to burn FF fuses with SBFE=1, even when operating the fuse controller from HS contexts. It is not clear what “secured burn” truly means, I speculate that there must be a software-only way to perform non-FPF burns even with SBFE=1, and we just don’t know what the “secured” adjective really means here.
Note PLM, HS, ucode, …; I am delving into using a bunch of NVIDIA-specific terminology in this section as the explanation gets deeper. For a really in-depth explanation of what these mean, I refer you to other sources such as Je Ne Sais Quoi - Falcons over the Horizon.
Importantly, as people have figured out on more permissive cards, it is possible to perform FF burns with SBFE=0! And as it turns out, achieving this state is how we achieve the GA100 unlock. After much trial-and-error, I have resorted to inducing this state via voltage fault injection, and I was able to achieve it. Let’s talk some more about voltage glitching.
Voltage fault injection
Much has been said about VFI, and I’ll leave the in-depth explanation to other sources. In short, applying brief pulses of low supply voltage will often cause unexpected behavior in integrated circuits. I asked GPT-6 Astra to design an STM32G4 based board that taps into the PWMVID signal on the CMP PCB. PWMVID is an NVIDIA standard for voltage regulators, and my glitcher intercepts the PWM signal emitted by the GA100 die, and replaces it with its own waveform fed into the MP2888B VRM driver IC. With my setup, I can induce the card’s own VRM to produce timed glitches for me, which is simpler than MOSFET-based setups and enables faster glitching than attempting to directly drive the PMBus.
The glitcher requires two connections to the PCB, ideally done with magnet/enameled wire. One wire taps NVVDD for voltage sensing, and another wire taps the PWMVID signal. The only other required step for the glitcher to function is the removal of a 0402 0ohm resistor, which will break the connection between the GA100 output PWM pin and the VRM IC. Finding where to place the taps is trivial by tracing the pinout of the MP2888B, specifically its PWMVID and VOSEN pins (the MP2888B shares a footprint with its sibling public chip MP2888A). Test points directly adjacent to the MP2888B enable relatively easy installation of the PWMVID tap.
With this tap in place, a single glitch attempt involves this sequence:
- Remove card power
- Apply card power
- Start a timer (“glitch timer”) as soon as NVVDD crosses a threshold
- Execute a proposed voltage waveform by issuing a PWMVID signal, aligned to the glitch timer
- Observe card behavior, repeat from step 1 as needed
My setup achieves steps 1/2 with a simple ACPI S0 -> S3 -> S0 transition, which can be done in a few seconds on a modern desktop platform. More intrusive modifications or expensive rigs can probably achieve a better experiment rate, but in my experience this setup suffices to unlock cards in somewhere between 1 hour and 48 hours of glitching time using the approach described later.
For the NVVDD threshold, the Astra-authored firmware uses an STM32 comparator to detect when NVVDD crosses 225mV, after which a tight DMA loop drives the desired duties on the PWMVID pin. After S0, the host inspects the card state and decides what to do next; if it involves another glitch, the glitcher board will be commanded over USB with a glitch pattern. Then the host induces S3 with an RTC timer to wake back up in ~3s (empirically derived period for decent stability).
Sometimes the host will fail to return to S0, I’ve remedied this with relegating bookkeeping and glitch campaign preparation to an SBC (Radxa Cubie A5E) which also can drive the motherboard power/reset button pins via GPIO if the glitch target host is unresponsive.
More specifics are shared in the GA100VFI repository if you’re interested. For now, let’s take a look at the different interesting states we can trigger via VFI, as well as the specific glitch state that we need to burn FF rows. To help illuminate the differences between each glitch state, I have built an empirical model of how the fuse controller starts up when voltage is applied. Note that without the RTL that implements the fuse controller, all we have are guesses. Here are the hypothesized boot stages:
- Sense RIR, as required by the fuse macro
- Sense (from fuse macro into readout register) control rows
- Latch control rows into control row-derived option words
- Sense remaining rows
- Latch regular fuse values into their option words
- Parse FF chain
- Latch FF chain values into their option words
These hypothetical stages are based on what I can actually read from the die: controller states, raw rows when CMD_READ works, the published option words, and whether the PRI ring can still reach the rest of the GPU. By looking at a few key values, we can tell glitch outcomes apart. Importantly, glitch patterns and outcomes are very much die-specific, so consider these example waveforms and responses to be just that, examples. Let’s take a look at 3 interesting glitch states.
1. All fuses sensed as zero
Some glitches make almost every published option word read as zero. In one captured state, 669 of 672 named option reads were zero; the other three were error responses. The controller’s CRC status was 0x00 (not parsed yet), the PCIe ID read as 2080 (the base GA100 PCIe product ID, does not correspond to a real retail product), and the GPU’s PRI ring was held in reset.
This state is consistent with a catastrophic failure on behalf of the fuse controller. The card comes up basically unusable, because almost all boot functions are disrupted by the all-zero state. However, interesting enough, the card trains at PCIe Gen4 natively! Some slightly altered variants may showcase sections of fuses being successfully latched, or containing garbled values instead of all-zeroes. I was not able to push any of these states towards an FF burn; in almost all of them the fuse controller is unreachable or dysfunctional.
2. RIR read disrupted
Reading the RIR data on the CMP 170HX 8GB reveals its exact effect: 15 noop repair instructions, and one write that changes the value of a fuse in row 18, whose option word we can monitor. Further, because the RIR sense is consumed internally by the fuse macro instead of directly by the fuse controller, we can observe a disrupted RIR latch by attempting to read the raw row - the observed bitflip remains consistent across the flipped option word as well as the raw fuse row. This sets an interesting chronological checkpoint in investigating die boot (RIR sense must happen prior to other fuse sensing), but is not a useful glitch in itself.
3. Goldilock’s glitch
The successful three-pulse state on my first card seemed to disrupt precisely the row0/1 based option words, while leaving other fuses and option words intact. In this state, all of the row0/1 derived option words are zero. The initial readbacks look like this:
At this stage, we are still not yet capable of issuing FF writes, because ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0. I am honestly not sure why ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM would ever be zero, given it’s 1 in retail boards, so this almost reads to me like a way to implement a glitch-detection canary (or at least it would be elegant to do so).
Fuse sensing happens one row at a time, with all 32 fuses powered for sensing with one line, meaning it is much more challenging for an attacker to make a single fuse appear as cleared or set. It would make sense, then, to include a “canary” fuse that disables security-critical features (like fuse burning) when it is cleared, because usually the attacker can only manipulate fuse sensing at the row granularity at most. So, when the row0/1 option words come up as all cleared, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM=0 stops us from burning any fuses.
However, take a look at what we have in this state: DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE=0. This word is normally 1, and it stops us from setting the EN_SW_OVERRIDE register to 1, which then lets us “shadow” most of the option words exposed by the fuse controller. Doing so involves writing to a register CTRL_OPT_*, corresponding to option word OPT_*, which then determines the effective value STATUS_OPT_*. This is what lets us shadow SBFE to be 0. But, even though we have DSOV=0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM turns out to be one of the option words that are impossible to shadow, even with DSOV=0. So it seems we’re stuck.
At least that’s what I thought, and I banged my head against the wall in this state for a while. Then I noticed that there is one fuse controller command I haven’t tried issuing yet: SENSE_CTRL. I had refrained from issuing this, because on the face of it it seems like all of the row0/1 (control fuse) derived option words would match their fused values, which would reset SBFE, turn off software option word shadowing, and leave us unable to fuse. To my surprise, when I issued this command, all of the control-fuse-derived options went to their fused value, except DISABLE_SW_OVERRIDE, which remained 0!
With DSOV=0, we can trivially set SBFE to 0, ENABLE_FUSE_PROGRAM is 1 because it matches its fused value, and we are off to the races! One wrinkle remains in that FUSEWDATA may have a locked down PLM, but with DSOV=0, we can just write 0 to OPT_SECURE_FUSE_WDATA_WR_SECURE to set the PLM to be all-ones, opening host access for fusing.
At this point, all that’s left to do is to calculate _DISABLE words that match the _DEFECTIVE values for the features we are interested in, and issue FF burns. Note that the occupied FF space and defective bits differ per die, so each burn must be die-tailored.
End results
Framebuffer unlock
On 8 GB cards with 80 GB intact (seems to be around ~90% of 8 GB cards from my limited sample size), the unlock yields the full 80 GB as a usable framebuffer. Multiple synthetic tests (writing pseudorandom words throughout the full framebuffer and reading them back after L2 invalidation) as well as real workloads (such as vLLM and SGLand) are fully functional. As mentioned, one of my cards has only 64 GB intact. In this case, the hardware unlock yields no framebuffer advantage.
Compute unlock
The 170HX is limited to 70 SMs out of the box. In practice, there are almost always >120 SMs non-defective on the die, and the unlock allows using them all. This results in a significant performance uplift, ~1.7x compared to the software-only 170HX unlock, and even an impressive ~1.2x over a retail A100!
PCIe generation
The only thing that stops cmpunlocker from advancing beyond PCIe Gen2 are the FF option words. With relevant bits cleared, Gen3/4 train and are confirmed to be fully functional. When combined with the PCIe decoupling capacitor mod, up to PCIe Gen4 x16 is attainable, matching a retail A100 PCIe variant.
NVLink
Zeroing out the OPT_NVLINK_DISABLE word is only one of the required mods for NVLink to actually work. Because the CMP 170HX PCB is missing the U11 IC (which connects PCIe 3.3v to an NVLink bridge pin), a stock board fails to bring up the reference clock generator on attached NVLink bridges. Simply bridging two of the pins on the footprint of U11 resolves this issue, although it removes whatever regulation or protection was provided by U11. Be careful if you’re bridging GPUs powered by different power supplies, as this will connect the +3.3V rails together unless you leave U11 unpopulated on some of your GPUs! The NVLink bridge works fine if you just patch U11 on one of the boards in the pair.
On the firmware side of NVLink enablement, there is a ROM check that needs to be bypassed with additional host-side commands. I’m sure your clanker can figure it out ;)
While investigating the NVLink unlock, I also found a few interesting quirks with NVIDIA’s NVLink implementation on the GA100. I will be posting a further blog post on this, so stay tuned!
Future directions
With arbitrary fuse burning, we mostly gain feature unlocks. Some security-sensitive options are shipped unblown by default, and burning them may lead to interesting footholds. But what’s more interesting to me are the deeper glitch states where many default-blown security-sensitive fuses sense unblown, enabling routes like debug HS execution, which grant unprecedented access to die internals.

Ukraine Pivots to Israeli-Italian Satellite Tech to Bypass Starlink Restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
08:26:40 UTC
17:26:40 KST

Ukraine Pivots to Israeli-Italian Satellite Tech to Bypass Starlink Restrictions
Ukrainian drone units adopt HiSky satellite terminals to maintain deep-strike capabilities after Starlink disruptions threatened critical military comms.
POLICY WIRE — Kyiv, Ukraine — The Ukrainian Armed Forces are actively diversifying their communications infrastructure to reduce a strategic dependence on Elon Musk’s Starlink service. This shift follows reports that restrictions on the military-grade Starshield network recently forced the cancellation of vital drone missions.
Russian military channels claimed on November 6 that Ukrainian units have begun utilizing specialized satellite terminals from the Israeli manufacturer HiSKY for their deep-strike operations. These 6-kilogram devices are seen as a functional alternative to the SpaceX-operated network previously dominated battlefield connectivity.
Russian engineers have been investigating the high precision and success of recent Ukrainian drone attacks on domestic oil refineries. The discovery of HiSky technology may provide answers regarding how Ukraine has maintained operational effectiveness despite fluctuations in its primary satellite access.
The move toward rival providers highlights the vulnerability exposed when a military relies on a single commercial entity for critical infrastructure. Recently, Ukrainian units experienced dropped connections and diminished operational speeds when Starshield services were suddenly restricted, causing significant tactical setbacks.
Competing satellite firms are now seeking to fill the void left by SpaceX’s perceived unpredictability on the battlefield. By integrating Israeli and Italian-developed technology, Kyiv aims to ensure that its strike capabilities are not subject to the corporate or political decisions of a single provider.
Reporting by Policy-Wire (PW)

Nvidia’s crisis has corporate governance experts reaching for the popcorn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
07:30:51 UTC
16:30:51 KST

Nvidia’s stock sank 5.47% on Tuesday, following a 4% drop on Monday, a loss of about 9.5% in two days, even though there wasn’t much news out of the company. CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly been trying to conduct business as usual after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The biggest development: the board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an internal investigation.
What comes next is mostly a guessing game, even for the people who study how boards are supposed to handle crises. Two corporate governance professors, Ann Lipton of the University of Colorado and Todd Henderson of the University of Chicago, say there is no real precedent for a CEO caught up in a suspected honeypot. And while they have views on what the investigation should ask, like everyone else, they’re watching to see how it plays out.
“There have actually been affair cases and sexual harassment cases,” Lipton said, but she was quick to add that she doesn’t know of previous cases that also involve potential national security compromises. Henderson, whose research interests include corporations, securities regulation, and law and economics, said much depends on facts few people have yet, including, most importantly, what, if anything, Alice Huang got out of Jensen Huang. (Secrets about Nvidia’s fabs or chip designs would matter to the Justice Department. Ordinary corporate information probably would not.)
Lipton described the investigation led by Nvidia’s independent board members, with their own outside counsel, as perhaps the most “standard” aspect of the whole affair so far. She also observed that an investigation will be “exactly as thorough” as the directors running it want it to be, which is also standard. Henderson made a related point about incentives, saying that Washington law firms that conduct internal investigations “know who pays their bills.” He didn’t suggest that’s happening here.
Lipton said she sees three lines of inquiry, including whether the law was broken, whether Huang violated Nvidia’s internal policies, and whether the board was misled, including how forthcoming he was and when he was on notice. It’s notable, as Wired reported Monday, that Huang hired a PR crisis firm known for handling sex scandals a full year ago. Of course, the driver could have been about the affair alone. It’s unclear when Huang learned Alice Huang was a suspected spy. The board said in a Sunday statement about the matter that Nvidia “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”
Henderson similarly stressed the importance of what Huang knew and when. He described two scenarios. In one, Huang hires a PR firm because an extramarital affair is embarrassing, without knowing who the woman is. In the other, he knows she is a suspected Chinese spy. “I think that’s very different,” he said. “If I were a board member and the CEO of a company with very sensitive technology was in that situation, I would be furious if they didn’t tell me.” Not telling the board that you have cancer “or that you’ve been sleeping with a Chinese spy,” said Henderson, “seems to me to be a fireable offense.”
Either way, Lipton expects shareholder suits, and she said two kinds are possible. Securities fraud, which she said is “only about lying,” is the most obvious, and as we reported yesterday, Nvidia is already facing a proposed class action lawsuit that alleges Nvidia and Huang misled investors by concealing Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang while describing dealings with her former employer as routine. “You can have as many affairs with Chinese spies as you like,” Lipton said. “You just can’t lie about it under the federal securities laws.”
A mismanagement claim under Delaware law, where Nvidia is incorporated, is much harder. Employees do “stupid or reckless or damaging things all the time,” she said, and courts don’t let shareholders sue each time. Shareholders bringing such a claim on the company’s behalf, known as a derivative suit, must first show the board is incapable of handling the problem, usually by proving directors are implicated or so beholden to the CEO that they can’t act independently.
Nvidia’s 10-member board has a track record of loyalty and deference to Huang, as outlined by a New York Times piece Tuesday morning. Still, the investigation those “independent” directors have announced with outside counsel makes that very hard. Lipton cited, for example, a shareholder suit over alleged mismanagement at McDonald’s several years ago, after its chief people officer was accused of harassment and its CEO had a relationship with a subordinate. Ultimately, the court found no reason the board couldn’t deal with the misconduct on its own.
Even if none of this ends up threatening Huang’s job, the episode raises other governance questions that don’t look great in retrospect. Nvidia is run with a famously flat structure, with more than 60 direct reports to Huang, and the company doesn’t appear to have a succession plan, which Lipton called “a danger for any company.”
Huang’s children also work at Nvidia. His son Spencer is a director of product management, his daughter Madison is a senior director of product marketing, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, works in business development. Some employees believe Huang is grooming successors, and when asked last month by Bloomberg whether Madison is in line for the job, Huang didn’t shoot down the idea, saying instead that it’s not something he’d wish on her.
Lipton called hiring the kids poor corporate hygiene, even though founders have long done it. (Kimbal Musk is on Tesla’s board because he’s Elon Musk’s brother, she noted.) Directors are supposed to act only for stockholders, but founders get more rope as long as the company is thriving.
Henderson similarly calls himself a strong “anti-nepotism person,” sharing that when his father worked at Westinghouse’s nuclear research lab, there was an absolute ban on hiring employees’ children. “Like, fine for them to be working there,” he said of Huang’s children working at Nvidia. But “the idea that one of his kids would succeed him” at a publicly traded company the size of Nvidia “seems crazy,” he added.
What Nvidia may have gotten more right, from a governance standpoint, is what it doesn’t have, which is dual-class shares. Huang reportedly owns about 3.6%, so he doesn’t control the vote. That makes him “easier to dislodge,” Lipton said, even though he is deeply integrated into the company in other ways.
Neither professor is rooting for or against Huang, each made clear. The simple truth is that with voting control on top of Huang’s holdings, the board would have even less flexibility. Without it, the board has a few more options.

Tim Peters has died
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
07:03:17 UTC
16:03:17 KST

I wrote this some time ago about Tim:
“”"
I worked with Tim and the rest of Python Labs for a couple of years in the early 2000s. Tim was a hugely positive influence on me throughout my Python career.
Before I had ever spoken to Tim, he was already legendary. He had worked for Cray Research writing compilers for supercomputers, and for Dragon Systems, writing speech-to-text software at a time when such a task was considered largely impossible. He took up Python on a lark in its very early days, becoming something like Python’s second real user after Guido.
Guido came to rely on Tim heavily. Tim will demur about this, but as far as I can tell, Tim and Guido were largely partners in the design evolution of very early Python, and before most important features made it in to Python, you could be sure that they had been examined from every angle, shaken, stirred, and thunk about very hard by both of them.
Tim often played the role of gatekeeper and polisher. You have Tim to thank at least partially if you were a refugee from Java or Microsoft languages, which made excuses for their sprawling verbosity, complexity, and poor readability. Python, at the time, made none of those and had none of that (it now does). Tim was crucial in ensuring it stayed that way during his most active years. He will claim differently, but, by my observation, it is no accident that Python ballooned in complexity after his exit as day-to-day core developer. Perhaps this was more due to the resignation of Guido as BDFL and the new Steering Council model, which was also coincident, but not having Tim around didn’t help either.
It was pure joy to read Tim’s Usenet and mail list posts, which were full of humor and good nature and measured positivity and not a little winking darkness. They somehow resonated with me on my journey from becoming a new programmer to a not-so-new programmer and they lit a path to becoming one on which you could be dramatically competent without becoming cryptic and insufferable. He was intensely knowledgeable, and unfailingly precise when arguing for or against some design change. But he was always gentle and patient and matter-of-fact, preferring to use humor and warmth rather than bile and authority as the currency in which he dealt.
Tim penned “the Zen of Python” (“beautiful is better than ugly…”) which can be seen via “import this” to this day. You can see a bit of his wonderful humor and style in the prelude to his introduction of the poem . His enthusiasm was infectious, and in the days when he was most involved, most everyone could be witnessed spouting Tim-isms (winks and “'lys” and whatnot).
When I did get the chance to work with Tim, he was just as influential. He had absolutely no pretensions. If I hadn’t already known him to be a computer savant, I would have assumed he was a biker or mechanic due to his long grey locks, full mustache and and working-class fashion sense. I would later find out that he had indeed worked at Harley-Davidson. I think he’s originally from Wisconsin, but an East- or West-Coaster not fluent in Midwest tongues could be excused for believing his disarming accent is Chicagoan. He seemed just like a regular-looking neighborhood punch-the-clock guy, not unlike all the mechanics and deliverymen and cooks and dishwashers and event staff I’d worked around as a kid and in my 20s. Except he was pretty much the smartest guy in every room he entered.
Tim’s demeanor and lack of pretense inspired me to think that despite my own lack of education and pedigree, with enough effort and grace, that I might become a half-competent programmer. And eventualy I did. But before meeting Tim, it was not a given. I was alienated by the pretensions of my community peers, and I was often reminded that they were not necessary only by Tim.
He was somewhat private. He could often be found with a pen and paper outside the building just standing alone, staring blankly off into space, presumably thinking about some mind-boggling algorithmic topic with which he had just been charged by our CTO, or perhaps mentally designing some aspect of a pet project, scribbling something every few minutes. He applied himself to our code, which included a custom database written in C and Python. He diagnosed and fixed a data-destroying bug in that byzantine codebase for our largest customer. This saved the account, and likely gave us enough runway for another year or so.
Everyone who worked there was in awe of his programming and debugging skills, and while we tried our best to let the poor man be, we often asked him questions, many of which were pedestrian and dull. I remember one of our teammates trying to engage him into a debugging session, claiming that some fault seemed to happen every six runs. He smiled winkingly and asked “have you grepped the source for six?” It was a minor jab but given the sincerity of the question, and the person from which it had come, it occurred to me at the time that it might not be the worst theory of debugging from which to start.
Tim was a Director of the Python Software Foundation from 2001 to 2014, bringing Python across an uncanny valley from a time where it was “interesting but ignorable” to “the planet’s default language” along with a cast of other incredible people. If you use Python, it’s not in small part due to Tim.
When I started my own open source projects, it was Tim whom I channeled during design discussions and sprints. I quite consciously used tricks I had learned from him to make the process fun and welcoming. Rather than become prickly about some technical conflict, I would try to use low-brow humor to defuse things and I would try very hard to learn everything I could about the topic before responding such that I could gain and rely on the respect of other contributors. I often failed, of course, because I’m not Tim, but I was at least a twentieth a Tim, and at the time, I think my co-contributors would have agreed that the projects I led were fun and worthwhile to work on.
It is in this way that Tim’s influence is likely most obvious to people today, because I’m not the only one who channeled him; any Python project started between 1995 and 2010 has a bit of Tim culture in it.
“”"
In sadness,
. C

US and Rest of World Must Follow China's Lead On Green Energy, Says John Kerry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

US and Rest of World Must Follow China's Lead On Green Energy, Says John Kerry (theguardian.com) 200
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe -- including the US -- must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year's climate summit. As Cop31 opens -- this year the climate conference is in Turkey -- there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest "five-year plan" adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to "actively participate in and lead global climate governance". Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220 billion, and they should grow again this year; the world's largest emitter is now the world's leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there. Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.  "The only country that has hugely accelerated is China," said Kerry. "The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day."
"[China] realized suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they're moving independently. There's been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump."
For autocratic states without free and fair elections, seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added. "They'll see where the market is going, and they will recognize where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal," Kerry said. "Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels."
He added: "The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they're going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That's the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable."

Greg Kurtzer's Ginux is now a userspace kernel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
05:25:54 UTC
14:25:54 KST

Ginux is a configurable userspace kernel for isolated Linux compatibility instances. It runs as an ordinary Linux process and places an explicit, versioned contract between managed workloads and the host kernel.
Important
Ginux began as an independent Rust kernel that booted directly through UEFI
and ran a Rocky Linux 10 userspace. That research phase is complete. Its
final source is permanently preserved on the
bootable-kernel
branch and at the
bootable-kernel-final
tag. Active development now continues here as a userspace kernel.
The standalone-kernel experiment proved that an AI coding agent, directed by an experienced human through architecture, gates, and executable tests, could construct a new kernel capable of running meaningful Linux userspace. It also made the limits of that result obvious.
Linux is much more than source code. It is a stable interface, a development process, a global community, vendor and hardware alignment, and decades of compatibility and operational experience. Reimplementing kernel mechanisms does not reproduce that ecosystem, and competing with Linux was never the goal.
The more useful result is the boundary the experiment exposed. Linux must preserve a broad userspace ABI; as Linus Torvalds put it, “And we simply do not break user space.” The kernel regression documentation records that rule. Ginux can sit above Linux and deliberately offer a smaller contract to each managed instance. Before a managed syscall has a host effect, Ginux decides whether to emulate it, perform a validated mediated operation, or deny it.
Put bluntly: Linux must not break userspace; Ginux is designed to break the full Linux ABI guarantee deliberately and selectively. A instance receives only the capabilities and interface behavior its approved workload requires. Every departure is intended to be explicit, versioned, reviewable, and tested, rather than accidental incompatibility.
This pivot is also a result of the development method. AI made it practical to build disposable but executable prototype code, test an architectural idea, learn from the running system, and carry the valuable parts into a better design. The prototype was evidence, not an obligation to turn every experiment into a product.
Host Linux kernel
  `- host systemd (real PID 1)
       `- ginux (ordinary trusted host process)
            `- instance contract
                 |- virtual processes and identities
                 |- virtual descriptors and kernel views
                 |- assigned devices and resources
                 `- managed Rocky Linux userspace
                      `- instance systemd (virtual PID 1)
Ginux supervises native x86-64 programs and intercepts managed syscalls before their host effect. Its central dispatcher resolves the instance contract and chooses one of three outcomes:
- Emulate: answer entirely from Ginux-owned state.
- Mediate: validate and translate the request, then perform a narrow Ginux-owned host operation.
- Deny: return a configured Linux-compatible error or terminate the task.
The current implementation includes:
- a security-focused x86-64 interpreter and a balanced native ptrace backend;
- strict, versioned instance configuration and lifecycle;
- a digest-pinned OCI root, immutable filesystem index, and bounded overlay;
- Ginux-owned process, credential, signal, synchronization, timer, and event models;
- virtual devices with explicit assignment, ownership, and revocation; and
- bounded virtual /proc, /sys, cgroup v2, mount, namespace, machine, and
boot-identity views;
- a host-shared network backend that remains syscall-mediated; and
- a pinned Rocky Linux 10 systemd baseline that reaches multi-user.target,
authenticates a managed console login, updates through Rocky's enabled
repositories, and shuts the instance down cleanly.
This is a named compatibility baseline, not a claim of complete Linux or
systemd compatibility. Its exact image, readiness marker, tests, evidence, and
limitations are recorded in
hdae/gates-done/9-systemd-baseline.md.
Ginux is also being tested as a containment boundary for AI agents and other automated software that can execute commands, modify files, open network connections, and start additional processes. Instead of giving an agent the host's complete Linux ABI, an operator can place its process tree inside a instance whose kernel contract exposes only the operations and virtual resources required for the task.
The research goal is a reviewable boundary spanning syscalls, ioctls,
filesystems, devices, networking, process authority, and virtual /proc and
/sys state. For example, a contract may allow an agent to read time, inspect
its own processes, and modify one assigned workspace while denying clock
changes, host filesystem access, unapproved network listeners, and unrelated
devices. Ginux can then audit the contract decisions made while the agent and
its child processes run.
This is an active verification target, not a claim that Ginux is currently a production-grade agent sandbox. The contract inventory, configurable policy, adversarial tests, performance costs, and escape boundaries are tracked through the HDAE gates and must be demonstrated before stronger containment claims are made.
The userspace-kernel idea is established research and engineering territory. Ginux explores a particular point in that design space:
Ginux does not promise the complete Linux ABI. Compatibility claims apply only to named contracts, workloads, and executable evidence.
The reference development environment is macOS arm64. QEMU TCG boots a pinned Rocky Linux 10 x86-64 host where Ginux runs as an ordinary unprivileged process. The host systemd remains real PID 1.
Check prerequisites:
make doctor
Prepare the pinned assets with explicit network operations:
make host-image-fetch
make image-helper-fetch
make instance-image-fetch
make systemd-image-fetch
Build and run the deterministic suite offline after the caches are populated:
make build
make check
make test
Inspect the latest completed capability directly:
make test-systemd       # cached image, external networking disabled
make test-multi-instance # two concurrent Rocky systemd instances and isolation
make bench-prepare      # one-time networked setup for the pinned benchmark image
make bench              # matched native/Ginux matrix plus mandatory budget checks
make bench-modes-prepare # one-time setup for the three-way dispatch comparison
make bench-modes        # native/selective/paranoid tables and graphs
make demo-gate-15       # bounded reproducible three-way comparison
make demo-gate-17       # operator-readable concurrent-instance isolation check
make test-systemd-live  # shared network plus real upstream dnf -y update
make host-run           # general interactive Rocky host with Ginux installed
make host-reset         # discard that host's cache, instances, and writable state
make demo-gate-9        # Gate 9 checkpoint through the same host workflow
Instance recipes select syscall control under [contract.syscalls]:
[contract.syscalls]
control = "selective" # default; use "paranoid" for all-syscall mediation
default = "deny"
allow = ["*"]
deny = []
selective is the default and permits direct host execution only
when the instance contract allows the operation and Ginux's versioned catalog
independently classifies it as direct-safe. Denials, virtual state, inspection,
translation, emulation, pointer or descriptor validation, and modified results
remain Ginux-dispatched in both modes. paranoid is an explicit opt-in that
sends every syscall through the Ginux userspace dispatcher before completion.
make bench-compare checks every row against the 4% native budget and, after an
accepted baseline is published under benchmarks/gate11/, against that Ginux
baseline as well. Environment mismatches are reported separately from
performance regressions. make demo-gate-11 runs a bounded human-inspectable
comparison and returns nonzero when a mandatory row misses its budget.
Gate 15 provides a separate characterization workflow across native Rocky,
selective Ginux, and paranoid Ginux. Native is the no-mediation control, not a
Ginux instance mode. The checked-in templates under
benchmarks/gate15/ fix the complete test protocol and
may be copied without editing scripts. make bench-modes produces paired raw
samples, metadata, a Markdown table, and an SVG graph under build/gate15/.
See Reproducible performance measurement for the exact
protocol, customization workflow, output schema, and interpretation limits.
make host-run boots the QEMU Rocky host and logs you into its ordinary shell.
Ginux is installed in PATH. The first create or import downloads and verifies
the pinned Rocky OCI image with live per-layer progress; later operations reuse the
cache. The writable Rocky host overlay persists across make host-run, ordinary
cleanup, builds, and tests, so cached images, instance definitions, roots, and
stopped status remain available. make host-reset is the explicit destructive
operation that stops the host and removes that overlay; the next make host-run
starts from the pinned clean Rocky image.
A complete first session is:
ginux create rocky
ginux list
ginux status rocky
ginux start rocky --attach
create starts from the documented default recipe. Use
ginux import NAME FILE to create or atomically replace an instance from a
self-contained recipe, ginux export NAME to print that recipe, and
ginux edit NAME to validate and atomically apply an editor session.
Instances are contract-locked by default. For an explicit maintenance window,
stop the instance, run ginux unlock NAME, perform the required maintenance,
stop it again, and run ginux lock NAME. ginux list and ginux status NAME
show the current state, and starting an unlocked instance prints a warning.
Unlocking relaxes configurable recipe restrictions only; Ginux still owns the
virtual kernel boundary, rejects unsupported authority, reduces host identity,
and applies NoNewPrivs. Lock state is host deployment state and is never
written into an exported portable recipe.
Syscall auditing is disabled by default with [audit] enabled = false. Add
--audit to ginux start to enable it for that run, or set enabled = true
to enable it for every start. Enabled audit records always go to the instance's
audit.log; they are kept separate from the attached console.
Existing recipes using mode = "stderr" or mode = "disabled" remain
read-compatible and normalize to the new boolean form when rewritten.
The instance specification supports typed recipe overrides, ingress and egress contract policy, volumes, virtual identity, and ordered pre-boot hooks. Host network attachment and translated ports are deployment settings, supplied as repeatable flags when the instance is created or changed:
ginux import web /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml \
    --network eth0:1 \
    --forward protocol=tcp,external_port=8080,instance_port=80 \
    --forward protocol=tcp,external_port=8443,instance_port=443
ginux set web \
    --network default \
    --forward none
Omitting --network uses the host's default network. Multiple flags are
validated and persisted atomically; an invalid combination changes nothing.
Hooks run only as
mediated instance processes; Ginux does not support arbitrary host-context hooks.
See Gate 9.75 instance specification
for the schema, precedence rules, examples, and verification targets.
The same instance file contains a self-contained hierarchical contract under
[contract] and its syscalls, filesystem, network, devices,
privileges, process, and kernel subsections. Syscall names accept bounded
globs compiled against the pinned catalog; explicit denies always win. The
contract is part of the instance rather than a separate operator object.
Validate and inspect the complete instance recipe before launch:
ginux validate /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml
ginux inspect /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml
ginux explain /etc/ginux/examples/rocky-systemd.toml filesystem.path.write
See Self-contained userspace contract for the syntax, precedence, migration behavior, and complete CLI workflow.
The attached terminal becomes the Ginux instance console. Log in as root with
password ginux, explore normally, press Ctrl-] to detach while leaving the
instance running, and run kill -RTMIN+4 1 as instance root to
shut down systemd and return to the host. Detached operation uses
ginux start rocky, ginux status rocky, and
ginux stop rocky. Exit the Rocky host shell to stop QEMU cleanly.
This stops the VM without deleting its persistent overlay; make clean resets
that host state. make demo-gate-9 uses the same operator workflow;
make run-systemd remains as a compatibility alias, and
make test-systemd-interactive is the automated regression.
The live test and interactive demonstration enable shared external networking. An upstream DNF update can take many minutes under QEMU TCG because every managed syscall is intercepted and audited. The offline systemd test uses only the prepared, digest-pinned cache.
Individual component and gate targets are documented in the Makefile and the
corresponding files under docs/ and hdae/.
The primary adversary controls a process inside an instance. The host kernel, hardware, Ginux executable and approved configuration, boot chain, and operator are currently trusted. The balanced native backend still relies on the host for ELF loading, address spaces, page faults, signals, scheduling, and ptrace; those remain host-kernel attack surface.
Ginux is research software. It has not received independent security certification, does not provide complete Linux compatibility, and is not ready for production workloads. Unknown contract operations fail closed, but current coverage and guarantees are limited to the tested gates.
The precise supported claims, retained supervisor authority, trusted components, exclusions, compatibility gaps, performance limitation, and reproducible boundary tests are documented in Security boundary and limitations. The tested concurrent lifecycle, virtual-state, root, contract, audit, and shared-network semantics are documented in Concurrent instances and isolation.
For agent containment, the protected object is the host and any authority not explicitly assigned to the instance. Ginux constrains the Linux processes in which an agent and its tools execute; it does not inspect model reasoning, secure an external model provider, or make untrusted code safe outside the enforced instance boundary.
The full intent, threat model, invariants, and gate plan live in:
Ginux is developed with
Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE):
human-owned product intent, architecture, constraints, and acceptance
boundaries combined with agent-executed implementation, diagnosis, and test
loops. Each approved gate records its scope, non-goals, acceptance criteria,
verification, evidence, and stopping point in hdae/.
The independent bootable kernel remains available for research and historical reference:
It is no longer the active development line. The code remains available under the repository's existing terms for anyone who independently chooses to study or fork it.
The name remains a joke in the same family as Linux: Ginux combines Linux,
GPT, and Greg. To keep the author's ego within its configured resource limit,
the G officially stands for GPT.
Ginux is available under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE and
NOTICE.
On x86-64 Linux, ginux launch <config> <root> [--result-file <fresh host path>]
executes [instance].init with the configured arguments and environment inside
the supplied host root directory. The bootstrap requires chroot and credential
change privileges, and a kernel with close_range (Linux 5.9 or later).
It drops to UID/GID 1000 before executing the workload. The configuration must
select profile = "balanced" and backend = "ptrace-native"; storage and device
assignments are not implemented by this command and are rejected.
[instance].workdir is optional and defaults to /work; / is also supported.
The bootstrap creates the working directory if its parent exists, then enters
it after dropping privileges. Init and working-directory paths are limited to
128 bytes and must be absolute without .. path components. Up to seven
arguments of 128 bytes each and eight NAME=value environment entries of
256 bytes each are accepted. Invalid or oversized input fails before launch.
Workload stdout stays separate from supervisor diagnostics on stderr. Only
stdin, stdout, and stderr are inherited by the workload. The launcher returns
the workload exit code, or 128 + signal for signal termination. Startup
failure returns 2; supervision or result-writing failure returns 1. Native
fork, clone, and subsequent exec are unsupported; fork returns ENOSYS until
child supervision is implemented. Non-x86-64 syscall ABIs and job-control
group stops fail explicitly. Audit output is capped at 64 KiB plus a truncation
notice. This path does not implement resource quotas from the instance metadata.
When requested, the result file is reserved exclusively before launch, with mode 0600 and a maximum path length of 512 bytes. Existing files are never overwritten. After completion, it contains one synced JSON object:
{"version":1,"outcome":"exited","code":0,"signal":null,"generation":null}
outcome is exited, signaled, or supervisor-error; only the relevant
code or signal is populated. Storage generations are not implemented, so
generation is null. A missing, empty, or malformed result is a protocol failure.
A failure to write, sync, or close the result returns 1 even if the workload
succeeded. Consumers should wait for launcher completion before reading it.
The focused Linux integration scenario consumes existing binaries:
make build
make build-launch-fixture
make build-gate1-fixture
sudo make test-gate1-setup
sudo make test-launch
sudo make test-native-supervision
The separate process-native <config> <executable> command exercises native
fork, clone, vfork, exec, threads, waits, termination signals, and pipes. It
executes a trusted host fixture as the caller, without chroot; it does not
require root on a host that permits tracing child processes. Configured
launch remains a separate entry point and does not yet use this process loop.
Process creation returns virtual identities, including clone TID cells.
Untraced, reparenting, namespace, and unsupported clone flags are denied.
Thread slots are reclaimed on exit. CLONE_FILES shares one descriptor table;
ordinary fork copies it, and exec unshares it before closing CLOEXEC entries.
Worker-thread exec preserves the group's process identity. Inherited host
files above stderr are closed before execution. PI futex operations and queries
for another task's robust list are unsupported.
Build the fixtures explicitly, then run their independent scenarios:
make build build-process-fixtures
make test-process-native
make test-process-native SCENARIO=shared_pipe
make test-process-native SCENARIO=thread_exec
The scenarios consume existing binaries under .artifacts/process, including
checks for syscall ABI dispatch, clone restrictions, descriptor inheritance,
thread reuse, successful and failed worker exec, signals, wait-status writes,
nonblocking waits, and vfork. The existing native fork fixture also runs. These
checks do not claim complete libc, job-control, or systemd compatibility.

It is no longer the active development line. The code remains available under the repository's existing terms for anyone who independently chooses to study or fork it.
The name remains a joke in the same family as Linux: Ginux combines Linux,
GPT, and Greg. To keep the author's ego within its configured resource limit,
the G officially stands for GPT.
Ginux is available under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE and
NOTICE.
On x86-64 Linux, ginux launch <config> <root> [--result-file <fresh host path>]
executes [instance].init with the configured arguments and environment inside
the supplied host root directory. The bootstrap requires chroot and credential
change privileges, and a kernel with close_range (Linux 5.9 or later).
It drops to UID/GID 1000 before executing the workload. The configuration must
select profile = "balanced" and backend = "ptrace-native"; storage and device
assignments are not implemented by this command and are rejected.
[instance].workdir is optional and defaults to /work; / is also supported.
The bootstrap creates the working directory if its parent exists, then enters
it after dropping privileges. Init and working-directory paths are limited to
128 bytes and must be absolute without .. path components. Up to seven
arguments of 128 bytes each and eight NAME=value environment entries of
256 bytes each are accepted. Invalid or oversized input fails before launch.
Workload stdout stays separate from supervisor diagnostics on stderr. Only
stdin, stdout, and stderr are inherited by the workload. The launcher returns
the workload exit code, or 128 + signal for signal termination. Startup
failure returns 2; supervision or result-writing failure returns 1. Native
fork, clone, and subsequent exec are unsupported; fork returns ENOSYS until
child supervision is implemented. Non-x86-64 syscall ABIs and job-control
group stops fail explicitly. Audit output is capped at 64 KiB plus a truncation
notice. This path does not implement resource quotas from the instance metadata.
When requested, the result file is reserved exclusively before launch, with mode 0600 and a maximum path length of 512 bytes. Existing files are never overwritten. After completion, it contains one synced JSON object:
{"version":1,"outcome":"exited","code":0,"signal":null,"generation":null}
outcome is exited, signaled, or supervisor-error; only the relevant
code or signal is populated. Storage generations are not implemented, so
generation is null. A missing, empty, or malformed result is a protocol failure.
A failure to write, sync, or close the result returns 1 even if the workload
succeeded. Consumers should wait for launcher completion before reading it.
The focused Linux integration scenario consumes existing binaries:
make build
make build-launch-fixture
make build-gate1-fixture
sudo make test-gate1-setup
sudo make test-launch
sudo make test-native-supervision
The separate process-native <config> <executable> command exercises native
fork, clone, vfork, exec, threads, waits, termination signals, and pipes. It
executes a trusted host fixture as the caller, without chroot; it does not
require root on a host that permits tracing child processes. Configured
launch remains a separate entry point and does not yet use this process loop.
Process creation returns virtual identities, including clone TID cells.
Untraced, reparenting, namespace, and unsupported clone flags are denied.
Thread slots are reclaimed on exit. CLONE_FILES shares one descriptor table;
ordinary fork copies it, and exec unshares it before closing CLOEXEC entries.
Worker-thread exec preserves the group's process identity. Inherited host
files above stderr are closed before execution. PI futex operations and queries
for another task's robust list are unsupported.
Build the fixtures explicitly, then run their independent scenarios:
make build build-process-fixtures
make test-process-native
make test-process-native SCENARIO=shared_pipe
make test-process-native SCENARIO=thread_exec
The scenarios consume existing binaries under .artifacts/process, including
checks for syscall ABI dispatch, clone restrictions, descriptor inheritance,
thread reuse, successful and failed worker exec, signals, wait-status writes,
nonblocking waits, and vfork. The existing native fork fixture also runs. These
checks do not claim complete libc, job-control, or systemd compatibility.

Ocarina of Time is even better if you use a smartphone app
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-11
05:08:26 UTC
14:08:26 KST

I never liked hunting for Golden Skulltulas in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The game has 100 of them tucked all over Hyrule, and even over my many hours with the N64 classic growing up, I can’t remember ever actually finding all of them, or even wanting to. Jumping into the Ocarina of Time remake, I expected to ignore the Golden Skulltulas once again. But while poking around Nintendo’s Zelda Notes companion app, I discovered that its maps are a huge help to tracking down all of the elusive golden spiders — and pretty much every other collectible in the game — and now I find myself constantly opening up the app to make sure I haven’t missed a secret.
Ocarina of Time is even better if you use a smartphone app
Finding Ocarina of Time’s hidden collectibles is a lot easier with the help of Zelda Notes.
Inside Zelda Notes, which is available in the free Nintendo Switch app (you don’t need a Switch Online subscription to use it), you can peruse a big map of Hyrule and tap on individual areas for a closer look. The app offers just enough direction to nudge me toward an elusive pickup; when zoomed in, the app drops icons on the map showing you the locations of different collectibles, and if you tap on an icon, the app will show a popup noting any items or special requirements you need to fulfill to be able to obtain it. There are also a bunch of filters you can apply, like swapping between the maps for child and adult Link and toggling categories of icons on and off.
For Skulltula hunting, the map has already saved my sanity many times. While exploring, I’ll often come across the telltale Golden Skulltula sound but have no idea how to get to the tricky spider, even with the help of additional chimes from the new Echo Gem Skulltula tracking item. But with a peek at the Zelda Notes app, I can pinpoint the exact location of where the Skulltula is supposed to be and if I need to use a certain item or change the time of day to be able to get to it.
I recently delved into the Shadow Temple, for example, and I couldn’t figure out how to get up to a Skulltula that I saw while coming down an elevator. But when I checked the icon on the Zelda Notes map, it said that I needed the Scarecrow Song to create a hookshot point, which I hadn’t gotten yet. As soon as I finished the dungeon, getting the Scarecrow Song was my first priority.
Zelda Notes has been useful for tracking down Pieces of Heart, too, which give Link more health once you collect enough. While running up and down Zora’s River, I kept seeing two Pieces of Heart on faraway ledges that I couldn’t figure out how to get to. (My memories of my extensive time with Ocarina of Time as a kid also failed me.) But tapping one of the icons on the Zelda Notes map revealed that I needed a Cucco to get to it — and suddenly, I understood why there was one of the chirping white birds near the entrance of the zone.
Yes, it can be annoying to have to open my phone and dig through an app to track down all of the Skulltulas and other objects of curiosity scattered around Hyrule. I play video games to try and get away from my phone, not look at it more. And sure, I could just look up an online guide, but that often means wading through walkthroughs of varying quality, trusting an AI summary, or scrubbing through a YouTube video. But with Zelda Notes, I’m usually in and out relatively quickly, putting down my phone after seeing a clue or an icon that pushes me in the direction of the next golden spider. I’ve already found more than 70 Golden Skulltulas, and to my surprise, I now want to hunt for the full 100.
